on behalf of the ppe group.– madam president, first of all i would like to congratulate mr mato and i would like to support this new proposal that aims at transposing into european law measures under the multiannual bluefin tuna recovery plan in the eastern atlantic and mediterranean as adopted by iccat. in order to rebuild tuna stocks, we need to follow certain steps. first of all, we have to set up a gradual reduction in total allowable catch levels. this is very important. but we also need to impose stricter fishing within certain areas and time periods and new minimal sizes. this is also important. finally, we have to reinforce the iccat scheme of joint international inspection. i agree that the rules should be applied in a uniform way in order to ensure a level playing field for all engaged in tuna fishing including, and most importantly, for non-eu operators. otherwise, if we think about it, if we apply different rules to foreign fleets, all efforts and restrictions applying to eu fishermen will have no results and it will seem that we are actually penalising our own fishermen. we have to make sure that we do not penalise our own fishermen by imposing on them stricter measures. with that, i would like once again to express support mr mato’s work on this file.
madam president! we all know that bluefin tuna is a particularly valuable fish, a special gift of nature. some have described it as a living, floating gold mine moving at breakneck speed and therefore, there is a need for wise and prudent policies to ensure that this species of fish lives on forever. it is not so good, because we know that this species is endangered, and therefore the european parliament has not only the right but also the duty to transpose the rules on the multiannual plan for the recovery of tuna stocks. a few brief remarks first, legislation must be clear, consistent and unambiguous on tuna conservation, recovery and fishing. secondly, there must be strict enforcement for all tuna fishermen, including, and perhaps above all, those outside the european union. third, the maximum limitation and even elimination of illegal, even criminal, tuna fishing.
in writing. it does not take a great deal of physical chemistry to conclude that excessive screw-down of diesel engine energy efficiency to reduce co2 emissions is accompanied by an increase in fuel combustion temperature. if a certain threshold is exceeded, i.e. 1800°c inside the combustion chamber, toxic endothermic compounds (nox) may be generated. i am in favour of the establishment of a committee in the european parliament to clarify who really made the mistake of imposing on the motor industry, without defining and precisely specifying the means of measuring emissions, environmental objectives which are unrealistic from the point of view of the course of physicochemical phenomena. the commission is also proposing to extend the scope of the directive to include the use of biofuels, and to extend the scope of the directive to include the use of biofuels. i believe that the fault for the volkswagen affair lies with the european legislators, i.e. the ep and the ec. nature, it has been found, is governed by other laws - the laws of physics and chemistry - and the course of processes and phenomena as a whole is not subject to the excessive ambitions of politicians and their legislative creativity.
member of the commission.– madam president, beginning with the question, i am really sorry that the honourable member of the european parliament, krisztina morvai, missed my first intervention because i was just talking about the importance of human rights and the importance of the rule of law among european values. the european union is based on human rights and the rule of law, so i think that when we talk about intercultural dialogue and when we talk about the role of education in democratic socialisation, we have to take into account those values as well, which means the universal validity of human rights in the european civilisation. i think there is a consensus that education plays an enormous role in democratic socialisation, and there is a consensus that if we want to make our democracies more cohesive and more efficient then we have to go beyond formal educational institutions and we have to map out all the opportunities in non-formal and informal education and in intercultural and inter—religious dialogue, and we have to map out the role of the family in democratic socialisation, in teaching democratic soft skills for our children, for the next generations. the ward report is a very important element and step in this long and pretty complex road. we are just at the start of that road and i am looking forward to working with you efficiently and, hopefully, successfully on this project.
in writing. in a multicultural society, dialogue is a desirable alternative to antagonistic relations between representatives of different cultures, to the way of education, to the dissemination of basic values. thus, attitudes of mutual respect and appreciation become a prerequisite for fruitful cooperation between nations. intercultural dialogue is essentially a two-way process, with benefits for both parties. the eu member states' programmes (tempus iii, mundus) promoting the mobility of young people, including academic teachers, are therefore a valuable initiative. and through shared educational platforms, we're experiencing a process of synergy between generations. in addition, through participation in volunteering, sport and art initiatives, there is a process of differentiation of individuals whose actions enhance the relationship and consequently facilitate teamwork. this cooperation allows us to deal much more quickly with social phenomena, such as violence, radicalism, racism, xenophobia. another flagship initiative is the european cities partnership, a 'europe for citizens'. its aim is to promote cultural, information and economic exchanges, so as to be able to co-create international activities at the grassroots. dialogue thus becomes a window on the world, whose strength is its diversity.
in writing. the motto of the european union, 'united in diversity', underlines the immense wealth of europe's cultural, social, linguistic and religious diversity. intercultural dialogue plays a major role in the harmonious coexistence of different cultural identities and beliefs in europe. the promotion of this dialogue cannot be the task of public authorities alone; it requires the involvement of the whole of society, including representatives of civil society, religious leaders, but above all the family, which is the basic cell of our social life. it is in the family that each of us begins to learn about the culture, values and norms of society, which is why the family plays such an important role in promoting dialogue between cultures. intercultural dialogue brings people and nations closer together, effectively prevents and helps to resolve conflicts, and promotes reconciliation. it allows us to better understand the differences between us. this is particularly important in the context of recent tragic and disturbing events in europe and the world. every effort should be made to promote this dialogue through the use of new technologies, including social media. this will help us to reach young people, who are particularly vulnerable to the distorted image of other cultures.

emphasis on the importance of better preparing graduates for the labour market. a real partnership between education and business is needed, and young people themselves need to be involved in all the activities that improve their situation on the labour market. good practices exist in this area, but they need to be disseminated. my report also highlights the role of smes in creating new jobs and the fundamental importance of entrepreneurship skills training from the earliest age and the promotion of entrepreneurship. in addition, the report highlights the role of key skills, including those related to new technologies, and the importance of combining theoretical training with traineeships and professional practices. the report also stresses the importance of making education and lifelong learning systems more flexible and of removing barriers to further education and retraining. it draws attention to the under-utilisation of skills training opportunities in the workplace. another important aspect is to level the playing field by supporting young people from disadvantaged groups, including from poverty-stricken families, migrants and young people with disabilities, in acquiring appropriate vocational and social skills and in realising their own potential. finally, i pointed out that the potential, talents, values, and priorities of young people raised in an era of rapid technological advancement are vastly different from those of the previous generation. i think this is one of the reasons why the potential of the younger generation is still not fully understood and used. it is therefore worth investing in programmes that help employers and employment services better understand the values, opportunities and potential of the younger generation. we'll be voting on this report tomorrow. i am confident that our work together will help to better target action to support young people's access to the labour market and that the findings of the report will inspire further work. the dramatic level of youth unemployment is one of the most serious threats to europe's social and economic future today.
in writing. one of the most important problems facing the european union for many years now is the huge unemployment among young people. the current problems have been overshadowed by the fact that more than 4.5 million people aged 15-24 are unemployed, and in some member states the unemployment rate for this age group is close to 50%. given the current refugee crisis, the problem of youth unemployment is likely to increase. if we are to avoid a build-up of problems and a kind of ghettoization, the education and training systems of the member states must adapt very quickly to this situation. on the other hand, we should also remember that young eu citizens will face new competition in the labour market and will demand even stronger support. the next few years will therefore be a very challenging one for both education systems and public employment services. tackling youth unemployment requires a focus on three pillars: formal education, career guidance and lifelong learning programmes. only by effectively combining these three systems and adapting them to the situation in europe will we be able to reduce youth unemployment in europe and effectively integrate and integrate hundreds of thousands of young refugees into the labour market.

rapporteur for the opinion of the committee on civil liberties, justice and home affairs.– mr president, i would like to thank everyone for the report, which is well-structured and with a balanced approach, including in the area of the competences of the committee on civil liberties, justice and home affairs, and with a clear message that we need digital harmonisation in europe. what does a ‘balanced approach’ mean? it means that we have not achieved the real turning point, to say that we need stronger solutions, more harmonised in some areas, as decisions on 5g spectrum development and text and data mining development have been scarce. on the other hand, however, we have made progress in the right direction, have begun working faster on the e—privacy directive and have established equilibrium between privacy protection, security needs and business opportunities in the era of big data. it shows that we understand how important data privacy is in the light of the data-driven economy. in that area, we need future—proof solutions. now we can start work on issues such as how to share data, what ownership of data means and how to make data much more secure, also using the solutions of security and privacy by design.
mr. chairman, please! i'm just pointing out the appalling noise and explaining the confusion because every market is uniform and the goods sold in it don't have to be uniform. if i read, for example, in the introduction, paragraph 1.1, that the creation of a digital single market can revive the single market, that is nonsense, because if we revive the market, it means that it exists, and if it exists, it cannot be created. this is a european union-wide nonsense. for example, we read that the internet has a huge impact on women's empowerment. why is there no mention of homosexuals, or zoophiles, or redheads? redheads, as we know, are fake, and the internet doesn't tell you if they're redheads or not, so the internet also promotes redheads' emancipation. ladies and gentlemen, this is a big deal, but we're voting yes because the free market is our priority.
mr. chairman, please! the creation of a fully integrated digital single market is one of the main priorities of the current european commission, driven by the need to make better use of the enormous potential of digital technologies to create strong growth and new jobs. it is estimated that this additional growth could amount to as much as eur 415 billion, opening the way for several hundred thousand new jobs. the obstacle, according to the legal affairs committee, is the rigid national regulations on the telecommunications market and the lack of harmonisation of copyright law, and in particular of its exceptions and limitations. it is therefore necessary to modernise copyright rules in the light of the digital revolution and changes in consumer behaviour, to create a level playing field where all economic operators offering their goods and services in the union are subject to the same, uniform principles, including data protection and consumer protection. intensive action is also needed to promote an entrepreneurial culture and more innovative business models.
in writing. ‒ the purpose of the proposal is to transpose into union law the measures contained in the multiannual recovery plan for bluefin tuna in the eastern atlantic and mediterranean, adopted by the international commission for the conservation of atlantic tunas (iccat) at its annual meetings in 2012 and 2014. the multiannual bluefin tuna recovery plan is a response to the significant decline in the stocks of this highly valuable fish. according to experts, the population of the atlantic sturgeon has declined by 83 percent in the last 50 years in the western atlantic and in the mediterranean. today, only 25% of the world's tuna population lives in these waters. in view of the above, i have supported the motion for a resolution.
in writing. ‒ proposal for a regulation of the european parliament and of the council on a multiannual recovery plan for bluefin tuna in the eastern atlantic and the mediterranean and repealing regulation (ec) no 302/2009. i strongly support the plan to restore bluefin tuna stocks in the eastern atlantic and the mediterranean. the application across the european union of all measures for the recovery of bluefin tuna is essential for a uniform and effective action in this area. the present proposal is to transpose into union law the technical measures contained in the multiannual bluefin tuna recovery plan.
in writing. ‒ during the post-world war ii economic boom, the consumption of fish - including raw and canned tuna - increased in developed countries, and for more than 15 years, japanese sushi and sashimi, which are made with bluefin tuna, have been extremely popular in europe and the world. the secondary effect of this trend is the depletion of tuna stocks in the eastern atlantic and the mediterranean, and the problem therefore directly affects the european union. the main countries involved in the tuna fisheries are spain, france, italy, croatia, greece, portugal, malta and cyprus. overfishing has led to a drastic reduction in the number of this species in the ecosystem. in 2006, the first long-term plan was drawn up, covering 15 years, to protect the resources and increase the tuna population. scientific research confirms that the tuna population increased for the first time in 2015. the high level of surveillance required by the eu (increased number and frequency of inspectors, vessels, aircraft and other means of control) has increased the tac for tuna by 20% compared to 2014. sustainable fishing, the regulation of stocks and fruitful cooperation between community countries are the source of success that has contributed to the development and protection of the valuable bluefin tuna species.
in writing. ‒ the report was supposed to deal with competition policy, but it deals largely with taxation. that's why i couldn't support the report. it repeated many of the recommendations contained in the taxe report. for example, it calls for a common consolidated corporate tax base, country-by-country public reporting for multinational corporations, access by the commission to data exchanged by member states' tax authorities, legislative proposals by the commission going beyond the oecd/g20 proposals on beps, and the establishment by the european parliament of a committee of inquiry to further investigate harmful tax practices (unlike taxe 2, which remains a special committee rather than a committee of inquiry). the report mentions the completion of the banking union (i.e. the third pillar, the european deposit guarantee scheme) and even the increase of the eu's own resources by transferring to the eu budget the recovered illegal state aid.
in writing. ‒ as author of the opinion, on behalf of the committee on international trade, on the 2014 report on eu competition policy, i am very pleased that the document adopted by parliament includes the provisions i proposed, calling for a significant deepening of international cooperation in order to effectively implement the principles of competition law. the ideal solution, which i strongly support, would be to work out a multilateral agreement on competition within the world trade organisation. i hope that will be possible in the next few years. as far as the european union itself is concerned, i believe it is extremely important to monitor more closely the implementation of the increasingly ambitious international agreements concluded by the community with third countries. we need to know whether the competition rules are being respected and whether the commitments made by the trading partners are actually being fully respected and enforced. what is also worth noting in the report adopted by parliament is the provision i have proposed on the need to equalise access to all resources, but with a clear emphasis on access to energy sources, as well as its transmission and transport. one of the most important factors in creating equity in the marketplace today is access to energy.
in writing. ‒ while ecr strongly supports intercultural dialogue and although this report contains positive elements in reinvigorating dialogue between communities, it has a number of serious faults which prevent us from approving it. primarily, the report fails to address the specificity and characteristics of cultural dialogue. while referring to eu fundamental values as they are set out in the treaties, it does not take into consideration existing pluralism in their interpretation, which should be acknowledged and respected. the report seems to neglect that genuine intercultural dialogue requires strong identities of interacting individuals or communities based on deep knowledge of their cultural canons, therefore a good knowledge of history, literature, music, etc. is indispensable. the spirit of the document suggests that a successful intercultural dialogue relies solely on opening up to other cultures by resigning from one’s own heritage – the rapporteur strongly objected to incorporating any references to the christian roots of the europe despite tabled amendments on behalf of several political groups. concerns were also raised regarding the form of the report – the text is incomprehensible and consists of lengthy, vague paragraphs made up of fragments that do not match.

in writing. children are not born with feelings of hatred towards others, these are emotions and behaviors that are formed as we grow up. it is therefore important to promote tolerance, equality and openness from an early age. people of different cultures, nations and views should come together as often as possible and learn that we are all human beings, with similar aspirations and concerns, and that only through dialogue and cooperation can we achieve this. the ep resolution aims to continue the dialogue agreed by education ministers after the november attacks in paris. the agreement recognises the need to make joint efforts to prevent and combat marginalisation, intolerance, racism and radicalisation, and to pursue equal opportunities for all. the ep resolution proposes concrete recommendations for action at all levels, including increasing the use of culture in external action and eu development programmes, and underlines the particular role of science, culture and active civil society in building a strong, resilient and open european society in the future. i therefore decided to vote in favour of the report on the role of intercultural dialogue, cultural diversity and education in promoting the eu's core values.
in writing. ‒ the report by julie ward comes at a very opportune time, as europe is faced with the question of how to deal with the problems of cultural exchanges, which very often result from simple ignorance, in the face of the wave of refugees. the role of intercultural dialogue in promoting the eu's core values should be strongly emphasised in this context. nor is there any doubt about the role that culture itself can play in the eu's external relations. a good knowledge of cultural realities, with a full understanding of their diversity, is an element that can prevent crises and a highly effective tool in resolving conflicts and promoting peace. the key element needed to achieve this will be the development of skills through the inclusion of relevant content in educational programmes, the provision of training and workshops. however, effective intercultural dialogue also requires financial support. i would therefore like to reiterate the importance of providing adequate funding for existing excellent examples of support for cultural exchange and intercultural dialogue, in the context of eu programmes such as erasmus+ and the partnership of cities funded by the europe for citizens programme. it is important that in the process of fighting for cultural diversity and education on the fundamental freedoms of europe, attention should be paid to improving the awareness and knowledge of not only the hosts but also the guests.
in writing. ‒ the report on the role of intercultural dialogue, cultural diversity and education in promoting the eu's core values is an attempt to summarise the legislative work on financial services, to address the gaps in the financial services legislative process and to highlight the resulting problems. the report also highlighted the effects of the individual legislative measures and the lack of a proper analysis of their interrelationships, as well as the lack of a full assessment of the overall impact of the legislation as a whole. i fully agree with the rapporteur that one of the main challenges for financial services regulation is the global competitiveness of eu legislation and eu financial sectors. the quality of regulation in the financial services sector is also important, and depends on the coordination, timeliness and transparency of the legislative process. i think that this initiative is justified and i have voted in favour of the report.
in writing. ‒ this own-initiative report is an attempt to summarise the legislative work on financial services, to address the shortcomings identified in the financial services lawmaking process and to draw attention to the resulting problems. in particular, it drew attention to the effects of individual legislative measures and the lack of a proper analysis of their interlinkages, as well as the lack of a full assessment of the overall effects of the overall provisions. it also addressed important new initiatives by the european commission, such as the investment package and the capital markets union, and indicated ways to achieve better results by building on existing financial services regulations that function effectively and efficiently. the rapporteur also believes that one of the main challenges for financial services regulation is the global competitiveness of eu legislation and eu financial sectors. the rapporteur notes that the quality of financial services regulation also depends on the coordination, timeliness and transparency of the legislative process. although the report touched on difficult topics such as the completion of the banking union and the participation of euro-area and non-euro-area member states, the rapporteur managed to find neutral language, which is why i have improved the report.
in writing. ‒ during the financial and economic crisis, the european union produced, under enormous time pressure, countless new rules and regulations on financial services, more than all previous financial services regulations combined. of course, the changes were necessary, given that the financial sector was the one that started the financial crisis in 2008. however, we should now look carefully at what goals have been achieved, which regulations are actually working, and which have been introduced too hastily and proved ineffective. the european parliament's report duly drew attention to the need to examine the consistency, accuracy, proportionality, added value and economic impact of financial services regulation. parliament also called on the european commission to prepare a comprehensive impact assessment of the new rules before the end of this year. it is essential to remove unnecessary provisions from eu legislation as soon as possible so that the european union can better serve its citizens and not create unnecessary barriers for consumers and businesses.
in writing. ‒ in 2014, the employment rate among them was less than 60% and was well below the europe 2020 target. in addition, most of those who are employed are part-time or in flexible forms of employment. one solution to this problem is to promote entrepreneurship among women. it should not be assumed that women do not want to be entrepreneurs, but rather that they are discouraged from doing so by external circumstances. the report we voted on indicates the obstacles that exist. however, i believe that the fundamental problem here is that there are still cultural constraints and that there are no real mechanisms to support women entrepreneurs. it seems, and the report emphasises this, that promoting social entrepreneurship would be a good solution. the available data show that women are much more likely to decide to start social enterprises, as they are more in line with their sensitivity and investment strategy. in turn, the experience gained in this sector of the economy will help some of them to move to the traditional economy sector. the added value is that social enterprises are much better able to respond to the challenges facing the eu economy and labour market today. europe will only benefit if we focus more on the social economy, both in terms of the level of employment for women and in terms of the instruments to address growing socio-economic problems.
in writing. ‒ entrepreneurship can be defined as a character trait, a set of skills, a way of thinking, planning and achieving one's goals. an enterprising person is ambitious, confident, and successful in pursuing his goals. in the labour sector, entrepreneurship most often means pursuing one's own interest company, partnership, enterprise as opposed to being employed by an employer. the eurobarometer data show that the entrepreneurship rate in the european union (12%) is still half that of china or the us (27% and 21% respectively), despite the elevation of entrepreneurship to a political priority. moreover, only one third of europeans who are self-employed are women. at the same time, women are more likely than men to start businesses this can be explained by the desire to reconcile work and private life, as self-employment is usually more flexible in terms of working hours, holidays and work at home opportunities. barriers to women entrepreneurship should therefore be removed, as stereotypes such as lower skills or lower resilience among women result in a lack of trust on the part of some entities, such as banks, which refuse to grant investment credit. such even superstitious thinking can still discourage women from starting their own businesses and lead to discrimination.
in writing. ‒ i fully support the report by barbara matera on the external factors hindering women's entrepreneurship in europe. women are less likely than men to participate in the labour market and to run their own businesses, and if they do, they are smaller and run in less profitable sectors. this is compounded by the large number of quasi-firms, created through the forced self-employment of women, who de facto perform work under the supervision of the employer. the report rightly points to the low availability of care services as a major barrier to entrepreneurship, but also to the disproportionate burden of housework on women. the report, citing the barcelona objectives including the availability of childcare services at a level covering at least 90% of children of school age, calls on member states to further invest in childcare infrastructure, which is a key tool for reconciling family and work responsibilities. the report also calls on the commission and the member states to review the law to eliminate the disadvantage of women entrepreneurs to wage workers, to invest in training, projects to create networks of women entrepreneurs, to offer monitoring and exchange of good practices and to combat gender stereotypes as key actions to promote female entrepreneurship. promoting female entrepreneurship, especially among the 45+ age group, is not only important for the quality of life of the women involved, but also through the use of their experience and work has a positive impact on the overall economy.
in writing. ‒ promoting entrepreneurship, which has always been at the top of the european union's political agenda, is becoming particularly important in an era of slow economic growth and the need to create new jobs. there is also no doubt that the freedom to conduct a business should be equally available to both sexes. unfortunately, women currently represent only 31% of entrepreneurs in the eu. this situation is directly linked to the existing barriers to women's full participation in economic life. to improve this situation, the ep report includes proposals for childcare and care for the elderly to help women entrepreneurs to reach their full potential and achieve a work-life balance. another issue highlighted in the report is the need to increase funding opportunities for women entrepreneurs. research shows that women use fewer external resources, such as bank loans, than men and tend to use more expensive internal financing. less capital, on the other hand, often means simply less chance of success. i therefore decided to vote in favour of the ep report on the external factors hindering european women's entrepreneurship.
in writing. ‒ i voted in favour of the european parliament resolution of 19 january 2016 on external obstacles to female entrepreneurship in europe (2015/2111 (ini)). entrepreneurship is essential for economic growth, employment, innovation and poverty eradication. the decision to enter the business world by women is the result of a clash of internal motives, including psychological and external factors, based on socio-economic determinants. the female entrepreneurship rate, which reflects female entrepreneurship in eu countries, stood at 31% in 2014. studies in this area are conducted much less frequently in women than in men. this is also why i support the establishment of a specialised institutional unit for women's activities in the eu. its tasks would be to support initiatives ranging from updating competitiveness information to introducing and verifying high tech. the so-called 'pre-incubators' are no less important. this project provides support for pre-business start-up and for the introduction of specialised training or exchange of experience among potential stakeholders. this would allow direct interactions to take place, resulting in a network of long-term business partnerships.
in writing. ‒ 5 million young people out of work, while 2 million vacancies are one of the eu's biggest challenges. the report clearly shows that skills development is a multi-dimensional process requiring a holistic approach and more flexible education systems that would allow for the development of knowledge and skills at all stages of a career. given the differences between labour markets in the member states, it is necessary to identify which level of management has the most effective tools to identify and describe skills needs. the report also called for the promotion of best practices and the integration of young people with disabilities in education and employment through investment in social entrepreneurship or financial incentives for organisations that employ them. it was also stressed that employment offices should be more active in removing physical barriers to access for disabled people to their services. young people without a job are one of the eu's biggest pain points and challenges that's why i voted for the document.
in writing. ‒ developing skills at all stages of a career is essential in today's world to get a good job. any changes in the training process should be adapted to the current needs of the labour market. i support skills strategies to combat youth unemployment. in particular, any attempt to improve science programmes and to promote the integration of young people with disabilities in education and employment is, in my view, essential in combating youth unemployment.
in writing. ‒ i voted in favour of the report on skills to tackle youth unemployment because i believe it is a good indicator of the key issues to address if we want to develop young people's potential to work in an innovative economy. first of all, the report highlights a major problem facing the european labour market today: the large skills mismatch between young people and employers' expectations and needs. as a result, although there are several million job vacancies across europe, many young people remain unemployed. therefore, swift, decisive action is needed to remedy this situation. in his report, mr plura tackled the important issue of learning to be an entrepreneur from a very young age. self-employment and starting your own business has great potential in combating unemployment. moreover, entrepreneurial skills are universal, they shape entrepreneurship and help people to find and do almost any job. it also welcomes the fact that the report duly emphasises the need for cooperation and coordination at all levels between education and training institutions, employers and non-governmental organisations. focus should also be placed on optimising the use of the instruments available at eu level: the youth guarantee, financial instruments and cohesion policy support.
in writing. ‒ in the labour market, young people are the first victims of the economic crisis. according to scientific research, the unemployment rate for the under-25 age group is very high in the eu countries: in its august 2015 publications, eurostat indicates that it is 20.4%, and in the euro area countries it is as high as 22.3%. germany (7%) has the lowest youth unemployment rate and is the only country where unemployment does not exceed 10%. the countries with the highest unemployment rates are the four southern european countries: spain (48.8%), greece (48.3%), croatia (43.5%) and italy (40.7%). in 2012, the european union responded to this problem with a plan called the 'eu employment package' to help young people access the labour market through a variety of measures. it is a series of guidelines to support job creation and improve employment policies. the main objectives of the programme are to reduce taxation of workers, increase net profit, create new jobs by mobilising eu funds, promote training adapted to the labour market and remove legal and practical obstacles to the free movement of workers. the package also covers the creation of a european labour market, economic development, promotion and support for self-employment, modern enterprises and start-ups. the report by our colleague, mr plura, supports these ideas, and i am also in favour of them.
in writing. ‒ education, including entrepreneurship, is a key element in tackling youth unemployment. however, education must be subject to market expectations and opportunities so that young graduates or vocational school pupils are able to enter the labour market more quickly and effectively. to achieve this, it is necessary to ensure closer cooperation between the education sector and business, and to involve young people and organisations representing their interests in actions to improve their situation on the labour market. the ep report rightly emphasises the need to promote high-quality traineeships or dual education, which gives young people the skills they need to pursue a profession and put them into practice. as has been well noted, a new generation brought up in an era of rapid technological advancement has different talents, expectations, and abilities than previous generations. it is therefore important that member states adapt their employment policies to the changing reality. i therefore decided to vote in favour of the ep's strategy on skills to combat youth unemployment.
in writing. ‒ the changing macroeconomic situation in the world makes it increasingly difficult to keep up with the expectations of a rapidly changing labour market. in line with the eu youth strategy, the european parliament points to close cooperation between institutions at local, regional, national, european and member state levels. it is considered appropriate that youth policy must be based on the promotion of activity, entrepreneurship, enhanced competence, mobility and flexibility in the potential labour market. the proposed measures to combat unemployment should be based on the facilitation of the harmonization of the education system while allowing for the possibility of being an active person. this is why the initiative to modernise the education system should be taken, and thus to adapt the curricula to the current and future labour market forecasts. another equally important element is the promotion of self-employment. actions to support initiatives and support individuals. the young people's community should have the opportunity to acquire and develop the necessary knowledge to set up their own businesses, to obtain financial resources, and to be able to meet their professional goals productively.
in writing. ‒ i support the report prepared by the european parliament's committee on employment and social affairs. this is an important report because we still have 24 million unemployed in europe, including 7.5 million young people who are neither in education nor in work. at the same time, there are over 2 million unfilled jobs in the european union. similar problems exist in poland and in my kujawsko-pomorskie province. many young people have qualifications that do not match the demands of the labour market. the report rightly emphasises the need for a more integrated education system with enterprises and institutions. there is also a need to develop wider skills in technology, engineering and mathematics, which are increasingly needed in a modern economy. in my view, eu measures to support education systems in individual countries and small and medium-sized enterprises should be a broader stream directed towards these very objectives.
in writing. ‒ the pace of the digital market has changed our reality and the way we look at industry and the competitiveness of european businesses. i see barriers in the organisation of the digital marketplace that are hindering their unfettered activity and further development. despite many obstacles, polish smes are making the most of this opportunity. however, the report contains a clause calling for the creation of a union-wide, common consolidated corporate tax base (ccctb), which i cannot support, especially in a report in which competitiveness is one of the main premises. taxes are one of the most important prerogatives of any country and although there are elements of the fiscal system that are subject to eu coordination (vat), i want this tool of state policy to remain in polish hands. first of all, it is a report on the digital environment in the eu. i cannot agree to the introduction of a postulate on this occasion which would lead to the loss of the possibility of conducting an active fiscal policy and, as a result, to a decrease in the competitiveness of the polish economy.
in writing. ‒ the pace of the digital market has changed our reality and the way we look at industry and the competitiveness of european businesses. however, the report contains a clause calling for the creation of a union-wide common consolidated corporate tax base (ccctb), which i cannot support, especially in a report in which competitiveness is one of the main prerequisites. firstly, it is a report on the digital environment in the eu, not on direct taxes, and this is one of the reasons why i cannot support a text that contains such a call. moreover, i cannot agree to a position which would lead to the loss of the ability to pursue an active fiscal policy and, as a result, to a decline in the competitiveness of the eu economies with the lowest cit rates. the argument that there is unfair competition in taxation within the union is an abuse and a one-sided interpretation of the situation by some member states, and the smaller member states would simply lose out on unification. finally, one of the reasons why i cannot support the inclusion of this provision in the final text is the result of past pressure on certain countries which have been accused of 'extremely harmful tax competition'. this is simply unacceptable to a sovereign member state with its own fiscal policy.
in writing. ‒ in the age of digital technologies, which are present in almost every aspect of our lives, legislation regulating the use, access and distribution of programmes and multimedia content is of great interest. after all, it is inevitable that this will affect, to a greater or lesser degree, almost all citizens, whether individuals, small and medium-sized enterprises, or large, multinational corporations. the effective use of digital technologies brings greater job opportunities, access to a wider range of products, diversified methods of rapid exchange of information and administrative simplifications. in may last year, the european commission published a communication entitled 'a digital single market strategy for europe' with 16 initiatives to be implemented by the end of 2016, which is supported and extended by the report we are voting on today. among them, the main emphasis was on harmonising the rules on online sales so that they apply in all member states, regardless of where goods are bought and sold. this 'cross-border' nature of the legislation will certainly make it easier for consumers to buy and possibly return or claim products. the digital single market should also mean a certain standard of quality for digital networks, the provision of internet access services and, in particular, the removal of restrictions on data transmission. it is difficult to imagine a future without access to the latest technologies, which is why we need to support digitalisation in all sectors of the economy.
in writing. ‒ the pace of the digital market has changed our reality and the way we look at industry and the competitiveness of european businesses. however, the report contains a clause calling for the creation of a union-wide common consolidated corporate tax base (ccctb), which i cannot support, especially in a report in which competitiveness is one of the main prerequisites. firstly, it is a report on the digital environment in the eu, not on direct taxes, and this is one of the reasons why i cannot support a text that contains such a call. moreover, i cannot agree to a position which would lead to the loss of the ability to pursue an active fiscal policy and, as a result, to a decline in the competitiveness of the eu economies with the lowest cit rates. the argument that there is unfair competition in taxation within the union is an abuse and a one-sided interpretation of the situation by some member states, and the smaller member states would simply lose out on unification. finally, one of the reasons why i cannot support the inclusion of this provision in the final text is the result of past pressure on certain countries which have been accused of 'extremely harmful tax competition'. this is simply unacceptable to a sovereign member state with its own fiscal policy.
in writing. ‒ the creation of a digital single market is crucial for increasing competitiveness within the european union. the community must create opportunities to compete effectively for a leading role in the technological race with the united states and the asian countries. the introduction of changes to remove barriers in the digital market will boost economic growth and job creation in europe, which is estimated to add an additional €415 billion to the eu's gdp. but above all, the digital single market will serve europeans, both consumers and businesses, through actions such as the removal of geo-blocking, the guarantee of more transparent copyright rules, the introduction of facilitation in the cross-border parcel sector, the development of new business models, and finally the introduction of vat-related facilitation for cross-border sales. given the enormous importance of the digital single market for the economic development of the european union, i have decided to support the european parliament's report.

in writing. ‒ this report is the final piece of work on the three technical adaptation procedures adapting to the new legal framework the provisions applicable to products in the field of personal protective equipment, ropeways and gas appliances. the new legal framework has largely harmonised the obligations of manufacturers, importers and market surveillance authorities, which will reduce the administrative burden and increase legal certainty for all those involved in the manufacture and supervision of products placed on the eu market. as regards gas appliances, i particularly agree with the requirements for maintenance by professional service personnel and the wording used in relation to carbon monoxide poisoning. the agreed text avoided the introduction of professional maintenance obligations for all gas appliances, including gas cookers for tourists, which are designed to be partly serviced by users, relying instead on national rules to provide a more common sense solution. as regards carbon monoxide poisoning, i fully support the work carried out by the rapporteur in this area to raise awareness of this problem. i voted to accept the report.

vice-president of the commission/high representative of the union for foreign affairs.– mr president, let me first start by saying that here we are clearly facing a kind of threat that probably was not clearly perceived or conceived of even six years ago with the lisbon treaty, because it is quite clear that we have an internal threat – let us remember that the terrorists had eu nationalities in this case – but with a clear external link, because there were references, links, training, resources, support that were linked with what is happening in syria and daesh. clearly the line between the external and the internal even only six years ago was much better defined than it is today. so this is the nature of the threats – and let me underline that this is also a reply to those of you, a couple if not more, who referred to the need to defend our borders. let us remember that the attacks in paris were unfortunately perpetrated by people who hold eu passports. so it is not just a matter of defending the territory from the outside, it is also a much more complex issue of how we secure our citizens, how we guarantee the safety of our citizens from a threat that is at the same time internal and external, and we have to put together different kinds of measures there. i think and hope that the global strategy we are working on will also help us to redefine a common direction on how to guarantee the security of our citizens in these times – times that are themselves new and different. having said that, let me reply to some specific points that were raised. first of all, the use of article 42(7) rather than article 222. obviously it is for single member states to take the political decision as to which article they want to invoke in terms of asking for assistance from other member states. but let me clearly compare the two articles in question. article 42(7) refers to ‘armed aggression’ or ‘armed attack’ – we have different linguistic versions in different languages – on the territory of a member state, while article 222 refers to a terrorist attack or a natural or man-made disaster. in terms of obligation, in both cases member states have an obligation to act. in terms of contributions, in the case of article 42(7) assistance comes from individual member states while, as some of you have underlined, article 222 also calls for mobilising eu instruments. in terms of implementation – and here comes what is i think the most interesting point for our debate in the future – article 42(7) leaves the implementation process open. here i observe that the guidelines you were somehow indicating would have been useful in 2012 were not produced. i believe that today we are seeing the implementation of this article, putting together all our resources, all our services and intelligence. this is something that we managed somehow between the decision that we shared with the french government to use article 42(7) and the moment when this decision was shared with the member states in the defence council, a period of more of less 24 hours – it was certainly a quick reaction from the european union services that we were able to gather at very short notice, but i believe the work that both our legal services and our structures that handle this level of assistance worked extremely well, as did the coordination between member states. but coming back to implementation, article 222 on the contrary foresees that the european union has a coordinating role because of the potential involvement of european union instruments. but let me say something that i underlined in my introductory remarks: even though the wording of article 42(7) does not call for any kind of specific role for the european union in terms of implementation, we decided jointly with france and all the member states during the council meeting of 17 december, if i remember correctly, to have all the relevant eu structures and institutions, including myself, directly involved at all stages of implementation. that was a political choice and i believe this political choice demonstrated the willingness of all of us to use this article as a way of strengthening the role of the european union in this field. there is one element that might seem technical but is, i believe, important. elmar brok mentioned this, namely the location of the requested action is different when it comes to article 42(7) compared with article 222, because in the case of article 222 assistance is in principle provided inside the territory of the member state to reinforce its capacities during the crisis, while in the case of article 42(7) france was clearly requesting assistance in external theatres. so i believe this was an element that was considered during those hours. indeed, there were other articles that could have been used apart from these two, because you all know very well that we have article 44 that has never been used and that would have implied eu-csdp action – a military mission, with some member states, the ‘willing’ member states the article says if i remember correctly, taking the responsibility in conjunction with the council to lead, on behalf of the european union, a csdp mission or operation. my political assessment has always been and still is, and i believe the council strongly supports this vision, that it is not and it would not be appropriate for the european union as such to have a military operation or mission against daesh. this is a political choice. this is not a technical use of the treaties, and i believe that also in this house most of you would agree with me in saying that at the moment – and the situation might change or might have changed years from now – i would not see a csdp role for the european union for a military intervention against daesh in syria and iraq. not while we have other forms of engagement of the european union, such as the implementation phase of article 42(7) in all stages, which is somehow an upgrade of the role of the european union institutions and structures compared with the wording of the article, which is a political sign. and on the other side, as you know very well, we have the diplomatic and humanitarian work and the work of the european union within the anti-daesh coalition when it comes to our global commitment against daesh and against terrorism. when it comes to the nato issue, let me say that for those member states who are also members of nato, eu mutual assistance is a complementary element to nato’s collective defence. this is clearly stated in article 42(7) which says that commitment and cooperation in this area shall be consistent with commitments under the north atlantic treaty organisation for those states which are members of it. so no overlapping, no competition, no distance or divergence, simply a complementary possibility. and let me also add in more general terms that in this first year and a couple of months that we have been together in office, in parallel, i as high representative of the european union and jens stoltenberg as secretary general of nato, we have strengthened the cooperation between nato and the european union in a very significant way. i would expect this to take even more concrete form as we develop our strategy from now until june, and as nato prepares for the nato summit at the beginning of july. the two processes run in parallel. obviously we have completely different paths, but these are communicating paths, and we exchange views, especially on those fields where our cooperation can be complementary for the benefit of all – for instance, in those fields where the european union has a clear and specific added value when it comes to cyber threats or cyber security. so there are fields of cooperation that are growing stronger and stronger. the french decision that the council has shared to call for article 42(7) was and is a clear sign, first that the european union can and should be seen as an effective security provider, first and foremost by its member states. second, it is a sign that solidarity is indeed part of our union. third, that all articles of the treaties can be used. and let me say on this that we do not need ideological debates or theoretical debates: first of all, we cannot afford theoretical debates at this time when the security of our continent is at stake; but we do not need ideological debates either, we need to put in place and use the instruments we already have, and we need to create the political conditions for doing this together, united, highlighting the added value of the european union also in the security and defence dimension where it can be an increasingly precious and vital tool to serve national interests, in some cases in a more effective way than a purely national approach. the european union has an added value in this respect. let me mention the 17 missions and operations we already have around the world that are an instrument and a tool for all the member states together to act in different theatres where, together, we work better than we would do alone or through other means. because there are specific dimensions where the eu instruments work better than a nato instrument or a un peacekeeping mission or other kinds of missions. this is already something that the european council unanimously recognises. both the european council conclusions, of december 2015 and june 2015, indicate clearly a sense of direction towards investing more in the dimension of csdp, and i am confident that also with the help of this house the necessary work, the political work we need to prepare, is going to be done to achieve the implementation of the treaty provisions fully and successfully and, let me say, for the safety, the security and the benefit of all european citizens.

in writing. the unanimous and full support expressed by all eu member states for france in the face of the tragedy that forced it to invoke the mutual defence clause is encouraging. the invocation of article 42 (7) teu is primarily a political act and the european council and the european parliament are the venues for political debate. any first use of a clause requires an awareness that it will be used in different situations in the future. it is therefore of the utmost importance that the present situation sets a precedent, but also that it sets out the procedures for applying it in individual cases. since no analysis or guidelines were available at the time of the activation of article 42 (7) teu by france, ad hoc action was necessary. however, there is a clear need to define practical steps, guidelines and procedures to ensure a common and effective response when a member state invokes a mutual defence clause. the role of the eu institutions in this procedure should be strengthened and should primarily involve the coordination of the assistance provided. to this end, the eu needs a permanent civilian-military headquarters at the operational and strategic levels, taking into account the existing capabilities of the member states. this structure would be responsible for strategic and operational planning, including mutual defence, in accordance with articles 42 (7) and 42 (2) teu and their future application in close cooperation with the relevant nato structures.

vice-president of the commission/high representative of the union for foreign affairs. – mr president, as you know, i have spent the most part of this year in office travelling the world, and in doing so i have had the chance to look at europe and our european union through the eyes of our friends and partners. when they look at us, they immediately think of two things: our economic strengths – even after the crisis, hoping the crisis is actually passed – and our work for human rights. let me take this debate not just as an opportunity to list the priorities we have at the un human rights council in 2016. let me also say a few words on how we wish to promote human rights all around the world, and what human rights are to us. i believe the main tools we have to support human rights worldwide are multilateralism and engagement with all the relevant actors and stakeholders. this is why the human rights council is so central. it is the place where resolute action can be agreed against grave humanitarian rights violations, and it is also the un central venue for forging new partnerships to advance human rights around the world. it is where we seek to promote justice and equality, as well as collaborative and inclusive approaches in the face of discrimination, repression and violence. as such, at hrc31 we will be prioritising two of the worst cases of human rights violations and abuses: the dprk, which you will be discussing tomorrow in this hemicycle, and syria, which we discussed yesterday. the dprk continues to be one of – if not the – most oppressive states in the world. the freedoms of expression, religion and movement are almost non—existent. hundreds of thousands of people remain detained in political prison camps and other detention facilities. many of these people have not been convicted of any internationally recognised crime. at hrc31, we will be co-presenting with japan a strong resolution addressing this grave human rights situation. the resolution will call for accountability and extend the mandate of the special rapporteur. it will also press for effective follow-up by the dprk to the universal periodic review process and for a resumption of reporting to treaty monitoring bodies. closer to us, syria is by far the world’s largest humanitarian disaster, with no parallel in recent history. our first priority in the current political talks is to allow humanitarian access to the largest part of the country. such focus will be reflected in the resolution on syria. the recent axis of aid in madaya was a positive step, but it is just a first step that needs to be followed by many others, and relevant ones. in the long run, peace in syria will require justice and accountability for all. putting together the pieces of syrian society will not be easy. reconciliation will need, first of all, recognition of the immense suffering of the syrian people. to this end, we will support further extension of the commission of inquiry’s mandate, which we also discussed in a previous debate this evening, as this remains the sole evidence—gathering tool in support of potential future justice mechanisms. the human rights council is also a place where positive developments can be recognised, so our other country-specific priority will be on myanmar/burma, whose historic elections in november are a much welcome step forward. we still have ongoing concerns, in particular with regard to ethnic and religious minorities. we will then present a resolution which recommends to the new government that takes office in april to take swift and bold action to address these issues, and which ensures continuing un scrutiny of the developments in the country. we will also be presenting two thematic resolutions: one on freedom of religion or belief to underline eu support to the fight against the religious intolerance in all forms and expressions – and again, we come back to an issue we discussed a few hours ago – and one jointly with a latin america and caribbean group on the rights of the child. on freedom of religion, we will also be organising a side—event where the special rapporteur will present the key findings in his report with the participation of civil society. this is in line with our belief that we could not discuss basic human rights without civil society representatives. throughout the whole year, the european union will keep working with partners to promote and protect the space of civil society and – let me stress this – the role of human rights defenders in un proceedings and in all countries. before closing, let me mention two further issues of particular importance for our work on human rights: the credibility of the un human rights forum, and our own credibility. the first lies primarily in the independence, integrity and effectiveness of the office of the high commissioner for human rights. the eu has been, and will remain, an important partner in staving off attempts to place its activity under the scrutiny or guidance of un member states. this is essential to preserve its credibility. the european union has also extended concrete cooperation to help the office of high commissioner perform its vital task, that is, to service all the hrc-endorsed mechanisms and provide meaningful assistance for the implementation of international human rights agreements. this includes political backing and financial support under the european instrument for democracy and human rights. let us come to ourselves. worldwide, we are perceived as a champion of human rights, and rightly so. sometimes this is a good perception, while some other partners have some doubts about our role, but this does not stop us. on the contrary, this motivates us even more. let me tell you that, over the past year, this perception has been challenged. the current events are putting us to the test. it is not just the refugee crisis, it is also the long-term effects of the economic crisis and the growing sense of instability for our citizens. they need to find a way out of the past crisis with a shift in policies that is significant and visible. these are clearly not easy times, but if we lose sight of fundamental rights for all inside europe, all can be lost before we even realise it. you, here in this hemicycle, represent half a billion european citizens. there are very few of you right now, but still. our entire political class faces a tough challenge: to make our politics reflect what is best in us – what is best in europe – and we have a choice. we can focus on our fears, foster them and let them tear this union apart, or we can bet on the values that made us strong, on our diversity, on our solidarity, and restart the engines of this european union. it is clearly no easy task, but it is one we definitely cannot fail.
