in writing. ‒ i have decided to vote against the request for legal aid for suspects or accused persons in criminal proceedings and for persons subject to a warrant in european arrest warrant proceedings. my decision is based on the fact that, although the text put to the vote is the result of tripartite negotiations, i do not see the need to extend the scope of the directive. the division of legal aid into 'temporary' and 'ordinary' does not seem appropriate either. for these reasons, i voted against. i believe that the legislation currently in force is sufficient.
in writing. ‒ decisions at eu level should be made in a rational and cost-effective manner. the directive in its original draft formulated by the european commission pursued this objective. it provided for the harmonisation of national legal systems in order to guarantee legal aid to persons in the first stage of criminal proceedings, when they may be deprived of the effective possibility of having recourse to a lawyer, and in proceedings following a european arrest warrant. however, the legal solutions provided for in the directive as it stands go further and are not based on primary law. the treaty on the functioning of the european union provides only for minimum protection, not for the establishment of universal criminal law. such a broad regulation does not serve to build the confidence of member states in the institutions of the european union. for these reasons, i voted against the resolution.
in writing. ‒ i voted in favour of a regulation which prohibits trade in certain goods which could be used for capital punishment, torture or other cruel, inhuman or degrading treatment or punishment. this is a very important regulation to improve the sense of security among citizens. it specifies the items covered by this regulation and describes the exceptional procedure for those equipment and goods which, in addition to being liable to be used for illegal purposes, are also legally applicable. for these reasons, i voted in favour.
in writing. ‒ regulation 1236/2005 prohibits the export and import of equipment and goods which are not intended for use other than for torture or the execution of capital punishment. they are listed in annex ii to that regulation. the same act requires that the export of equipment and goods which are suitable for the above purposes but which also have other legitimate uses be subject to special authorisations. such goods are assessed on an individual basis. in 2011, regulation 1236/2005 was amended to control the export of substances that can be used in lethal injections during execution. the tripartite text introduces a system of prior authorisation for the provision of brokering services and technical assistance in respect of goods listed in annex iii or iiia. the supply of intermediation services and technical assistance related to goods listed in annex ii shall be prohibited. it shall prohibit the transit of goods listed in annex ii and of goods listed in annexes iii and iiia. it shall prohibit the advertising and promotion of goods listed in annex ii. it allows member states to adopt or maintain additional national measures restricting certain ancillary services in respect of goods listed in annex ii. it shall set up a coordination group within which experts from the member states and the commission shall exchange information on administrative practices. it shall apply the urgency procedure with regard to annexes ii, iii, iiia and iiib and shall introduce a review clause. i hereby endorse the report.
in writing. ‒ the eu regulation of 2005 has previously regulated the prohibition on the sale and export of equipment which could be used for capital punishment, torture or inhuman and degrading punishment. but it did not address key issues, including the prohibition of the promotion and advertising of tools used to torture people. the new regulation will ban the promotion and advertising of goods that are clearly used for execution or torture, such as electric chairs, automatic infusion pumps used for poison injections, leg chains or spiked sticks. the ban will also apply to arms exhibitions and fairs organised within the territory of the european union. i believe that the european union should not in any way facilitate the practice of torture and the use of the death penalty by providing tools that can be used for this purpose. the document therefore rightly includes provisions prohibiting the movement of such goods through the eu, even if they are destined for third countries. moreover, the regulation properly addresses the issue of transporting objects that are designed for other purposes but may be used for torture. under new eu law, carriers will be obliged to stop transporting items if they know they could fall into the wrong hands.
in writing. ‒ export controls are not just a tool for external trade. it can also effectively promote the protection of human rights in those states which are recipients of goods and services potentially used for the execution of the death penalty, torture or other cruel, inhuman or degrading treatment or punishment. the consistency of union export controls in this respect should be ensured, inter alia, by updating the list of tools which should be subject to such controls. regulation 1236/2005 on the prevention of torture also covers the export of equipment and goods which may be used for torture, although this is not their exclusive use. their export should be subject to special authorisations. the proposed amendments to the regulation also allow member states to adopt or maintain additional measures restricting goods-related ancillary services (e.g. advertising, transport, financial services). the regulation will undoubtedly strengthen the european union's responsible role in combating the death penalty and torture worldwide. i am in full support of this resolution.
in writing. ‒ the current regulation entered into force on 30 july 2006. it was intended to prevent the supply of goods to end-users who could use equipment or goods originating in the eu area for torture or capital punishment. as ten years of experience have shown, such cases have unfortunately occurred. the main error was that the existing regulation, while restricting the sale of goods, did not block the transfer of technology which was then used by non-eu countries. i believe that technical assistance providers from companies based in the european union should not be able to profit from the marketing of technologies that could cause human suffering or death. i therefore support the draft new regulation which would prohibit any entity registered in eu countries from providing technical assistance if the equipment, goods or technology it sells could be used for torture or capital punishment.
in writing. ‒ i voted in favour of the strategic cooperation agreement between europol and china, which concerns the exchange of information excluding personal data. it should be noted that china is currently a country of origin, destination and transit in the fight against organised crime. the agreement covers important issues such as: sharing expertise or the results of strategic analyses and advising and supporting on specific investigations. i voted for it because i support any action that aims to improve safety.
in writing. ‒ the strategic operational cooperation agreement between europol and china concerns the exchange of operational, strategic, technical or classified information. importantly, however, it excludes the exchange of personal data. this cooperation will therefore include expertise, general situation reports, results of strategic analyses, information on investigative procedures and crime prevention methods, training activities, as well as advice and support in specific investigations. china is a major player in organised crime: facilitating illegal immigration, trafficking in human beings, drug-related crime, counterfeiting of the euro, infringement of intellectual property rights, corruption in sport, and cybercrime and money laundering. in addition, china is home to organised crime groups with significant influence in europe, which fully justifies the establishment of cooperation between europol and china. in my opinion, the conclusion of a strategic cooperation agreement with china is essential for the fight against organized crime. it will improve its effectiveness and contribute to the intensification of international law enforcement cooperation.
in writing. ‒ the conclusion of an international agreement with a third country or an international organisation must be approved in advance by the eu council and the european parliament. the strategic cooperation agreement between europe and china concerns the exchange of strategic, operational, technical or classified information. the exchange of personal data is also involved in its termination. however, due to the strategic nature of the agreement, personal data will remain confidential and the information exchanged will relate to general situations, strategic analyses, crime prevention and investigative procedures. cooperation with china is particularly important as it is considered to be the origin of organised crime groups responsible for organising illegal migration, trafficking in drugs, weapons and live commodities, cybercrime, corruption and counterfeiting of money. and effective action against organised crime is particularly important in an era of increasing terrorist attacks.
in writing. ‒ china is an increasingly important country of origin, destination and transit in the fight against organised crime, such as facilitating illegal immigration, trafficking in human beings, drug-related crime, counterfeiting of the euro, infringement of intellectual property rights, corruption in sport, and cybercrime and money laundering. in addition, china is home to various powerful organized crime groups. the agreement between china and europol covers expertise, general situation reports, strategic analysis results, information on investigative procedures and crime prevention methods, participation in training, and advice and support in specific investigations. this agreement will help fight crime and increase security. i hereby endorse the report.
in writing. ‒ china plays a critical role in the fight against organised crime. in recent years, they have become a country of origin, destination or transit relevant to the objectives of criminal organisations. their activities also threaten the security of europe, inter alia, by facilitating illegal immigration, trafficking in human beings, drug-related crime, euro counterfeiting, cybercrime and money laundering. the strategic agreement between europol and china provides for the exchange of expertise, strategic analysis, information on investigative procedures and crime prevention methods. it also provides opportunities for training, mutual advice and support in specific investigations. importantly, the agreement will not include personal data. it will also help to combat crime and increase the security of eu citizens. for these reasons, i am in favour of a strategic agreement between europol and china.
in writing. ‒ i have decided to abstain on the resolution on the future of acp-eu relations after 2020. the european union's relations with the acp countries are of great importance and the objectives of this agreement must be clearly defined. i think that the resolution in its present form is too general, and that it refers to political dialogue, development aid and economic and trade cooperation. i feel that these are general guidelines that need to be worked out, and i have therefore decided to abstain.
in writing. ‒ i voted in favour of the neuser report on the future of acp-eu relations after 2020. i am convinced that work on the future partnership between the acp states and the european union after the expiry of the cotonou agreement in 2020 must continue, as this is in the interest of all concerned. but we have to think about what the best choice is for the nature of the relationship after this contract expires. i believe that the union's relations with the acp states could take the form of an umbrella agreement which would define a more general, global framework for our relations based on dialogue on issues such as the achievement of the sustainable development goals, climate change and migration, while allowing for a parallel strengthening of relations with individual regions or sub-regions based on more specific agreements. we also have to think about the future of the economic partnership agreements, because it is not clear whether these agreements will be able to exist independently because of the reference to the cotonou agreement. however, i think that the epas have proved their effectiveness in regulating our economic and trade relations and no one has any doubts about the validity of their continuation. finally, i would like to stress that the new agreement between the european union and the acp states must continue to promote democracy, the rule of law and human rights.
in writing. ‒ the acp-eu partnership agreement is the most comprehensive agreement between developing countries and the european union. since 2000, it has been the cornerstone of the eu's relations with 79 african, caribbean and pacific (acp) countries. the cotonou agreement expires in 2020, and the main objective of this resolution is therefore to establish a new relationship between the eu and the acp countries in order to improve the efficiency of cooperation and adapt it to new challenges. the resolution sets out the future acp-eu relationship in three main areas: political dialogue, development cooperation and economic and trade cooperation. calls for the fight against poverty and inequality and the promotion of sustainable development to remain the overriding objective of acp-eu cooperation. it also believes that the new agreement must be a political project based on the principles of ownership and must clearly eliminate the donor-beneficiary mentality. the private sector is an area to be considered as it can play a key role in the development process and contribute to its financing, protecting investments with respect for people, traditional property and uses and the environment in line with the un guiding principles on business and human rights. i hereby abstain from voting.
in writing. ‒ the cotonou partnership agreement between the african, caribbean and pacific states and the european union needs to be reformed to make it a more effective cooperation platform that responds to the challenges of the 21st century. there is no doubt that 40 years after the cotonou agreement, eu-acp cooperation has not produced the expected results, especially when compared with other partnership agreements to which the eu is a party. it is therefore necessary to analyse first of all the effectiveness of the cotonou partnership agreement so far, the results of which should form the basis for further action. the ep report rightly emphasises that partnership should be based on a political and economic project, not on a donor/beneficiary relationship. it was also noted that economic partnership agreements are an essential element for the development of these regions, while bringing benefits to european businesses and citizens.
in writing. ‒ the cotonou partnership agreement, signed in 2000, governs the cooperation of 79 developing countries in africa, the caribbean and the pacific with the european union. the agreement expires in 2020, which requires a new legal framework for the eu's relations with these countries. the resolution outlines future relations in three main areas: political dialogue, development aid and economic and trade cooperation. i agree that tackling poverty and inequality remains an important objective of acp-eu cooperation, as does promoting sustainable development with respect for the environment. sixteen years after the cotonou agreement, the development of a new framework for relations with developing countries requires reflection. we should break the donor-beneficiary relationship. it should be borne in mind that the political situation in the acp countries has changed considerably since 2000. since the beginning of the century, little has been achieved together on global challenges, including security, and the acp-eu joint institutions have been ineffective and have not produced concrete results. the financing of further cooperation is also an important issue that needs to be considered. i doubt that the proposal for future relations presented in the report meets these needs. i therefore abstained.

vice-president of the commission. – mr president, i would like to thank everyone for this fruitful discussion we are having here right now. if i can just agree with jens rohde that time was too limited to broach all those difficult questions within one minute or even four minutes. it is practically impossible. so let’s remember from where we started. a member of the european parliament, viviane reding, made a proposal and then we started to decrease roaming surcharges. but just one and a half years ago we were faced with the ‘5+5+5’ proposal: five minutes in five days in a year, ‘roam like at home.’ and people had to be happy about this proposal. we had hot debates and we were able to find a solution. thanks to this, roaming surcharges have decreased by 75% since this may. this is the first year people have said that they did not feel as if somebody was murdering their wallets when spending their summer holidays in other countries. in comparison with 2009 prices, we can say that the cost of roaming surcharges for calls, and sms messages have decreased by 92%, and even by 96% for data. today, many of you said that that we are bullish with regard to roaming surcharges. it is not a done deal yet and finalising the whole process is very complicated. as was mentioned by mr pereira, member states are in very different situations. in southern countries operators had to make investments to provide services to tourists visiting those countries only during the three summer months. it means that those operators are not able to get revenues during the other nine months. of course i am simplifying the situation. it means they have the right to ask for higher prices. and this is the reason why they have blocked this wholesale reform. there is now a blocking minority in the south and also in the north. what is wrong in the north? nothing is wrong, but, as miapetra kumpula-natri knows, in finland for example, for the same price you can get 100 times as many gigabytes than in hungary. while the average consumption of gigabytes in the european union is just one gigabyte per month, in finland it is 10 gigabytes per month. nevertheless, i think if this pattern of trips made by europeans during the year does not change then the majority of service providers will survive. it means we have to prevent abuse of the system, because people will not start to travel just to avoid high roaming surcharges. so fair use policies are, of course, important. as we know, we decided to withdraw this proposal based on daily limits. according to eurostat, just 0.1% of all trips last longer than 92 days. so practically, financially in real life this is not an issue, and it was not an issue. we have made new proposals based on residency, and i think they are better proposals. but we have to deal with wholesale prices. today, i still think eur 50 for one gigabyte is too much. it is too much, and even the proposal we made from the european commission – eur 8.50 per gigabyte – still leaves space to decrease wholesale prices. we have to find a good compromise which allows us to protect those investments made in southern countries to provide services to tourists and also to protect those consumers in scandinavian countries, for example, who love those generous offers with really affordable prices. so – as i said – i am sorry to say that is not yet a done deal. the european commission, member states and the european parliament have to work together to find the right balance, and we have to be keep our promises. we have to abolish roaming surcharges in the european union. i am looking forward to a fruitful cooperation with you.

in writing. i welcome the progress of the legislative work in the council, which recently adopted the full consolidated text of the draft regulation establishing the european public prosecutor's office. the creation of this agency will be the culmination of many years of debate and efforts by the european parliament and the commission to equip the european union with powers to protect its own budgetary interests in criminal matters. however, before the prosecutor's office can start its work, there are still a few issues that need to be resolved. the new pif directive, which clarifies the scope of the prosecutor's office's competence in this area, should be adopted as a first step. the important dilemmas which arose during the legislative work in the council (adequate legal basis, vat) and which blocked this process seem to have been resolved by the court of justice in the taricco case. it is also necessary to complete the reform of the judicial cooperation body in criminal matters, eurojust, with which the public prosecutor's office is to be closely linked under the treaty . the recent european parliament and council regulation on europol will provide the olaf with significant support in the exchange of operational information. these are the preconditions for the council to enter the final stage of setting up the office of the prosecutor, which will, as we know today, operate in a more structured form of enhanced cooperation.

in writing. the situation in syria, the further implementation of migration policy and the strengthening of border controls, as well as the strategy towards trade agreements that could have a significant impact on eu industry, are the main issues to be addressed at the european council in brussels in october 2021. concrete action is needed to pave the way for the implementation of effective migration policies. strengthen border guards in countries protecting the union's external borders. europe is part of a globalised world and should be better prepared to seize the opportunities offered by migration, especially in the face of an ageing population. nevertheless, it is essential to prevent and reduce illegal migration. this requires strengthening the eu's strategy to combat human trafficking and smuggling and deepening cooperation with the countries of origin and transit of migrants. the new management of the schengen area must also ensure a higher level of security. in the context of trade agreements, although the commission is in favour of the swift implementation of the canada trade agreement (ceta), i think that the first thing to do is to dispel the doubts that it raises in our societies. there is a need for broad consultation and for real safeguards to protect, for example, the steel industry in europe.
in writing. ‒ i fully support peru's accession to the 1980 hague convention on the civil aspects of international child abduction. the convention, signed by 93 countries, regulates the legal custody of children and gives legal effect to the laws of the country where the child is habitually resident. this is a very important regulation, for today more and more marriages are breaking up and, unfortunately, there are even cases of kidnapping. i voted in favour because no country that meets the requirements can be prevented from acceding to such an important convention. i also think that austria and romania should agree to this as soon as possible.
in writing. ‒ the hague convention of 25 october 1980 establishes a system of cooperation between states in resolving cases of abduction of children abroad. the purpose of the convention is to resolve such situations at international level by establishing courts competent to deal with such disputes. in this case, the law of the country where the child resides is applicable. in addition, the convention establishes a system guaranteeing the immediate return of a child abducted. today's vote reflects our desire to see as many countries as possible accede to the convention. many eu citizens are from peru, and children with links to that country will now be protected from illegal abduction.
in writing. ‒ report on the proposal for a council decision authorising the republic of austria and romania to give their consent, in the interest of the european union, to the accession of peru to the 1980 hague convention on the civil aspects of international child abduction. the hague convention of 25 october 1980 on the civil aspects of child abduction is a document of particular importance, since it establishes a system enabling contracting states to cooperate in resolving cases of child abduction abroad by a parent or legal guardian. it is equally problematic in such situations to determine the court with jurisdiction to grant custody of a child to a parent or guardian when each parent or guardian is a national of another country. the convention aims to address this problem at international level by establishing that only the courts and laws of the state in which the child resides have jurisdiction. the convention also establishes a system to guarantee the immediate return of a child who has been abducted. as many eu citizens are from peru and children have links to the peruvian community, which puts them at risk of illegal abduction, it is important that parliament approves this proposal to protect children across the eu.
in writing. ‒ the hague convention on the civil aspects of child abduction is an instrument of particular importance. first, it avoids prolonged uncertainty about the child's legal status. it is accompanied by a situation in which the child's parents are nationals of two different member states and a dispute arises as to which of them should be granted custody of the child and which court should decide on the matter. it is undoubtedly in the best interests of the child that this matter be resolved as soon as possible and that he be returned promptly and safely. in view of the accession of peru to the convention, a council decision authorising austria and romania to give their consent to such accession is necessary. this will allow the convention concluded between peru and the whole of the european union to enter into force. the hague convention has already been ratified by all the member states of the european union and dozens of other countries. the accession of another country deserves our approval and support, which is why i voted for the resolution.

in writing. ‒ i voted in favour of a resolution on the eu's global objectives and commitments for food and food security in the world. i'm glad that the amendments proposed by my group have been incorporated into the text of the revolution. addressing hunger and malnutrition is very important, and i welcome the text of the resolution which refers not only to immediate measures but also to long-term measures, such as the creation of sustainable agriculture that is resilient to climate change and food systems that can feed the world's population. the importance of increasing investment in this sector cannot be overlooked. i voted in favour of the resolution because it spells out the action to be taken to combat malnutrition and hunger.
in writing. ‒ the world's growing population is increasing the demand for food, and its scarcity is leading to hunger and poverty. malnutrition is mainly seen in children and takes the form of disorders in the body associated with stunted growth or low body weight, slowing down of natural development processes, general deterioration of health. in some countries, hunger is a serious problem, leading to an estimated 15 million deaths worldwide each year. rational food production and distribution are therefore essential to minimize this problem. to this end, support should be given to smaller food producers and a sustainable, efficient and climate-resilient model of agriculture should be promoted. social security should be provided to citizens in order to protect their basic food needs. modern food production and distribution systems must be able to feed the entire human population, estimated at 8.5 billion by 2030. the eu must therefore do everything it can to ensure that these objectives are met.
in writing. ‒ in the near future, food security and food supply will be a challenge due to increasing pressure on resources. the world's population is projected to increase significantly by 2050, which will require increased food production, reduced food waste and increased global availability, particularly where access is currently limited. it is essential to promote nutrition education programmes in schools and in local communities to promote healthy eating habits and a culture of responsible food purchasing. from the point of view of global food security, support should also be given to small farmers. the growing awareness and expectations of consumers about food and its quality and impact on human health can also be an opportunity for small family farms.
in writing. ‒ the european union's policies and actions for sustainable development have a global impact. an important test of this responsible role is to contribute to the fight against world food shortages. i agree that this requires eliminating systemic problems. hunger and malnutrition are often caused not so much by a lack of food as by its improper distribution. one third of all food produced is subsequently wasted. as the resolution rightly points out, more support is also needed for small farmers and local agriculture. ensuring access to land for the local population and countering mass land purchase practices is crucial. it is also essential to call on the european commission to increase these investments, which will directly address the problem of child malnutrition. member states should consistently support steps in the identified directions. i voted for this resolution.
in writing. ‒ i voted against the resolution on the european public prosecutor's office and eurojust. the group i belong to has always been against the establishment of a european public prosecutor's office because, in my view, as in the opinion of the other members of the group, it would violate the principle of subsidiarity. i am also not in favour of the establishment of a european criminal justice system. i believe that the fight against abuse and the resolution of disputes should be carried out within the existing legal framework. for the reasons i have just mentioned, i voted against.
in writing. ‒ according to the latest analyses, the loss of vat revenue across the union in 2014 was an astronomical €159.5 billion. it is therefore necessary for the eu, and all member states, to take action to prosecute and discourage abuses against the eu's financial interests, thereby protecting taxpayers in all member states contributing to the eu budget. in this context, the proposal to create a european public prosecutor's office to reduce the current dispersion of national law enforcement agencies to protect the eu budget seems most appropriate. the resolution rightly pointed out that a clear and unambiguous set of powers and procedures for the eppo should be developed. i believe that the creation of a european public prosecutor's office to combat the tax losses suffered by all citizens is necessary, which is why i have decided to vote in favour of a european parliament resolution on this matter.
in writing. ‒ in the light of article 86 tfeu, the council may, after obtaining the consent of the european parliament, establish a european public prosecutor's office. it would investigate and prosecute those responsible for misuse of eu funds. the existence and the shape of the eppo raise a number of doubts. until now, only national authorities were empowered to investigate and prosecute perpetrators in the field indicated. first, it appears that the member states could achieve the objective of combating fraud affecting the financial interests of the union within the current framework of coordination and cooperation. the provisions concerning the eppo need to be assessed in the light of the principle of subsidiarity. the european union should not seek to create new universal criminal law regulations. secondly, the analysis of the pif directive also raises doubts. it should be stressed that 90% of vat fraud is perpetrated against member states. it is not obvious that crimes in this area should be the domain of the union, the competence of a new supranational body. the european public prosecutor's office should be a collegiate structure, working closely with the member states. in the further work on the establishment of this body, the presidency of the council must have time to consider these concerns and comments. i therefore voted against the resolution.

in writing. ‒ on the resolution on the need for a european reindustrialisation policy in the light of the recent caterpillar and alstom cases, i decided to vote against. the resolution is due to the mass layoffs announced by both caterpillar and alston. the first company will see 10,000 job cuts worldwide. the company's declining sales are due to a global slowdown in oil production. alston, which plans to end its 130-year-old tradition of making trains in belfort, will offer its employees jobs elsewhere despite the layoffs of some 400 workers. the situation of the two giant companies caterpillar and alston should make us meps think about how to counter such situations, but i do not think there is a need for a european reindustrialisation policy, which is why i voted against.
in writing. ‒ one of the eu's key achievements is the creation of a competitive and single common market with the potential to attract investors, sustain strong value chains, create jobs and grow. the economic growth generated in these conditions directly translates into numerous sectors of the economy and the living conditions of people, who gain a wide range of opportunities in terms of employment and choice of residence. the social market economy model adopted in europe aims to ensure citizens' access to the labour market, social security and economic growth, which also involves respecting moral and ethical principles of conduct towards employees. however, the increasingly frequent problems, such as those currently being discussed in the ep, are another signal that should mobilise action to protect jobs in europe by making us more competitive in an increasingly globalised world market. to this end, it is necessary to pursue the re-industrialisation of europe consistently.
in writing. ‒ on 2 september 2016, caterpillar announced a major global restructuring plan, which includes the closure of the gosselies plant, resulting in the redundancy of 2500 direct employees and the threatened employment of around 4000 subcontractors. alstom's management took a similar decision by transferring its railway production activities (400 jobs) from the belfort plant to the reichshoffen plant, which is equivalent to the closure of the former plant. however, these are not the only production sites to be restructured in europe. further redundancies are likely to occur at alstom's plants in spain and italy and at caterpillar's plant in northern ireland. european industry is facing global competition. many third country companies export products with lower production costs to the european market, often with the political and financial support of their governments. in order to remain competitive and able to invest in europe, and to meet social and environmental challenges, eu companies are often faced with difficult decisions that have the greatest impact on their employees. it is therefore necessary to develop a european strategy for the main industrial sectors in europe in order to create a more favourable market environment and to maintain high quality employment, expertise and investment in europe.

madam president! at the last plenary session, president juncker, in his state of the union address, stressed that our agriculture is a very important part of the european community. i can't argue with that. our farmers grow and produce the healthiest, most diverse and safest products. it is therefore essential that this highest quality is maintained and protected at the next steps in the supply chain. the safety of food contact materials is one of the decisive factors here. this is a very complex issue and can be a major challenge for packaging manufacturers. it is therefore also important that the rules in this area are clear. i think the 2004 regulation provides a good legal framework. however, it is concerned that special measures have so far been adopted for only four of the 17 substances listed in the annex to the regulation. i believe that greater harmonisation of rules at european union level would have a positive impact on the level of food protection and consumer safety and, consequently, on the functioning of the common market. as with the rules on plastics, the new specific rules should address the issue of recycled materials, as they can potentially pose a different type of hazard. this includes, for example, accidental contamination from previous uses of packaging. the second issue, which the rapporteur rightly drew attention to, is the degree to which existing legislation is implemented and enforced in the member states. the commission should first examine the difficulties encountered by national authorities and manufacturers and should make efforts to facilitate their implementation and compliance with these regulations.
in writing. implementation of the regulation on materials intended to come into contact with food. it has long been known that not only the composition of food but also the packaging of food affects our health and quality of life. the researchers found about 170 chemicals in the packaging, such as: biosphenol a, phthalates, styrene, triclosan, formaldehyde, and pfcs (perfluorocarbons), which migrate freely into food and then have a significant impact on our hormonal balance, causing obesity, diabetes, neurological and inflammatory disorders, and cancer. in addition, no one nor the packaging manufacturer or the food is obliged to indicate the chemical composition of the packaging, and furthermore, the potential cellular or hormonal changes caused by these chemicals are not taken into account in the routine toxicological analysis, which raises serious doubts as to the correctness of the currently existing chemical regulatory procedures. it is therefore essential that legislation be adopted as soon as possible to mobilise packaging manufacturers to remove substances harmful to health from the packaging production process as well as from the food itself as soon as possible.

in writing. ‒ the agreement for global climate action was adopted at the 21st conference of the parties (cop 21) on climate change in paris in december 2015. the aim of the agreement is to keep the global average temperature rise well below 2°c above pre-industrial levels and to continue to strive to limit the rise to 1.5°c. the agreement also aims to ensure that the tipping point for maximum emission levels is reached as soon as possible, so as to achieve balanced greenhouse gas emissions and removals in the second half of the 21st century. in the context of the preparations for cop 22, to be held in marrakesh from 7 to 18 november 2016, it is appropriate to consider what action should be taken by the european union and individual member states to ensure that the key elements of the paris agreement are fulfilled without harming the competitiveness of european industry. the imposition of increasingly stringent climate requirements and the successive obligations imposed on industrial enterprises in the european union are leading to a reduction in their competitive advantage on the global market. some companies will move their operations outside the eu to save their profitability. others will go bankrupt or severely limit their activities in europe. the european union should therefore play a leading role in the fight against climate change in this process, provided that it is global and not confined to europe.

in writing. ‒ i supported the report on the implementation of the regulation on materials intended to come into contact with food. i justify my decision by saying that i see it as a good move to give parliament a greater role in resolving the discrepancies between the different chemical regulations. i support the general wording of the report on endocrine disruptors and bisphenol. that's why i voted yes.
in writing. ‒ we all have to deal with materials that come into direct contact with food: the dishes we use to eat our meals, the accessories we use to transport them, the packaging in which the finished products are sold. we often consider the ingredients and properties of the food we eat, and we choose items that we believe are safe for our food and thus do not harm our health. as food safety is a priority issue for eu policy, materials intended to come into contact with food are subject to restrictive eu rules, currently contained in regulation (ec) no 1935/2004. the safety requirements set out therein cover seventeen different materials, for which specific measures may be adopted. however, at union level, emergency measures have been adopted for only four types of materials: ceramics, cellulose, plastics and so-called 'smart materials'. for other materials, member states may adopt special provisions at their discretion. this situation unfortunately leads to the emergence of different product safety standards, disruption of the internal market, loss of competitiveness and higher food prices. it is therefore necessary to harmonise the rules, both as regards production standards and regular checks on food (including feed, which seems particularly important in the context of the asf epidemic). this will protect the health of consumers and improve the functioning of our market.
in writing. ‒ i believe that there must be clear and consistent procedures at eu level for food contact materials, especially as food can be one of the most important routes for people to be exposed to chemicals. we know that materials that come into contact with food can behave in different ways depending on their composition and properties. some toxins are released by heat, others by cold temperatures, and even in the refrigerator, toxins can be introduced into food. therefore, the control procedures for such materials must be subject to continuous review, as health should be a priority value for all of us. in support of these amendments, i voted in favour of the report by christel schaldemose on the implementation of the regulation on materials intended to come into contact with food.
in writing. ‒ food is recognised as one of the most important sources of human exposure to chemicals. therefore, the safety of food contact materials should be carefully assessed, as these substances can enter the products we consume. materials intended to come into contact with food include products such as packaging and containers, processing machinery, kitchen equipment, cutlery and utensils. it is estimated that there are about 15 000 different substances in food contact materials. the experts point to the need to urgently address the shortcomings in the implementation and enforcement of existing eu legislation, as the degree of enforcement varies widely. further harmonisation of the legislation on materials and articles intended to come into contact with food could help to ensure a uniform high level of protection of public health.
in writing. ‒ food packaging, kitchen equipment and utensils are used on a daily basis. some materials intended to come into contact with food and used in large quantities may be harmful. they are therefore subject to the legally binding rules laid down in regulation (ec) no 1935/2004. that act provides that more specific safety requirements may be adopted for specific materials. so far, such rules have been developed for only 4 of the 17 types of materials. i also agree that we should improve existing legislation on risk assessment and ensure better enforcement. i voted for the resolution.
mr. chairman, please! it is worrying that the single market is one of the areas where we see the highest number of complaints and violations of eu law. in 2014, more than 600 complaints were received and more than 160 infringement cases were initiated in this area. of course, not all of them are necessarily valid, but they do point to a problem. union citizens and businesses are very often confronted with a situation which they consider to be a breach of union law. i therefore agree with the rapporteur that an easily accessible online complaint form should be created. it will allow for effective detection of breaches of union law. another very important issue is whether, within the internal market, law should be regulated by directives or by regulations. i think the answer is not clear. on the one hand, regulations ensure a more uniform implementation of legislation, which can prevent the voluntary implementation of eu rules that often leads to protectionism. on the other hand, directives allow for greater consideration of the specificities of individual member states. the european commission should analyse both of these aspects in even more detail before deciding which legal form to use. this approach will certainly improve the application of eu law.

in writing. ‒ the european commission's annual report on the transposition of european law into the legal order of the member states is an important element in the construction of a harmonised legal area in the european union. i supported the report because it provides a clear analysis of the situation and makes specific recommendations, taking into account the subsidiarity aspect. timeliness and accuracy of transposition are essential for the coherence of the internal market and are in the interest of the citizens of the european union. delays or other irregularities in the implementation of european law may trigger a breach of implementation procedure, which includes a support and negotiation phase, but is gradually becoming more restrictive and may result in a judgment of the european court of justice and financial penalties for the member state in the event of evasion of implementation obligations. in the last 5 years, the eu pilot early warning system has reduced the number of infringements and a number of decisions have been taken to reinforce this approach to improving the effectiveness of implementation by setting up dedicated websites with a database of opened cases and dedicated complaint forms for individual businesses and citizens. access to information for all europeans and broad consultation of the law at an early stage are key to creating legislation that makes life easier, not harder, for citizens in all member states, and as such will be more efficient and better implemented than less consulted.
in writing. ‒ in 2014, the european commission received almost 4 000 complaints about alleged breaches of eu law, and acted on a quarter of them. this means that many countries still fail to meet their treaty obligations and either fail to implement eu legislation or implement it incorrectly. the timely and correct transposition of community legislation into national legislation and a clear national legislative framework should be a priority for member states in order to strengthen citizens' trust in the legal system. unfortunately, the eu institutions are also to blame for breaches of eu law, often setting unrealistic deadlines for implementing legislation, which makes it impossible for member states to comply with them. moreover, as the document indicates, the european commission should, from the outset, monitor effectively and in a timely manner how eu law is applied and implemented.
in writing. ‒ the report notes a decline in the number of infringement proceedings against member states. the european parliament does not have full information on this procedure and the outstanding cases. i think more committees should be involved in enforcement matters to better control. given the limited knowledge of members of this procedure, it is difficult to assess whether the lower number of infringement procedures reflects better compliance by member states with union law. however, i certainly support the effort to set realistic deadlines for the transposition of eu legislation into national systems. member states should have the necessary time to carry out checks and consultations before implementing directives. however, the principle of subsidiarity and proportionality should be respected in the application of eu law. these amendments were rejected during the drafting of the report. i also feel that the issue of the impact of eu law on competitiveness has not been adequately addressed. for these reasons, i abstained.

madam president, as we know, the aim of this proposal was to harmonise the approach to the enforcement of customs legislation and particularly to sanctions for infringements. at the moment, customs rules across the eu are the same under the union’s customs code, but when those rules are infringed, enforcement follows 28 different sets of legal rules and administrative traditions. that creates inconsistency within member states and can generate uncertainty for businesses. i am happy with the text that we are going to vote on this week. first of all, there will be no fixed minimum sanction for minor infringements, and secondly, for both minor and serious infringements, the financial fine should be imposed as a percentage of the duties evaded. the report also allows for the possibility, where the nature and the gravity of infringements so require, for member states to impose criminal sanctions in accordance with national laws instead of non-criminal sanctions as provided for by the directive . i believe that with this text we are ready for further negotiations with the council and the commission.

member of the commission. – mr president, first of all, allow me to congratulate the rapporteur on this comprehensive, balanced and deep analysis of the issue of human rights and migration in third countries. no state or organisation can escape from its obligations under international human rights law to protect and ensure respect for the human rights of migrants, irrespective of their status. we live in a world of seven billion people, with dramatic demographic imbalances, where inequalities are still growing. migration is here to stay. migration is the new normal and is now an integral part of our political dialogue with partners, very much in line with the global strategy. it took a while before europe accepted its responsibilities, but we are finally doing so. since 2015 our vessels have saved hundreds of thousands of lives in the mediterranean. operation sophia is disrupting the traffickers’ networks and bringing the smugglers to justice. in turkey, in lebanon and in jordan we are helping over half a million syrian children go back to school. the protection of the most vulnerable – the women and children – is at the core of our action in each and every initiative we take. we remain the largest development donor and humanitarian actor. we are, despite criticism, leading by example. faced with so much human suffering, we need to respond and we are responding. but we know there is no quick fix to the issue of migration. our new partnership framework (pf) approach reflects just this fact. it is an ambitious and innovative comprehensive approach, fully embedding migration in our overall foreign policy. it is not, as some wrongly believe, only about return or readmission. it is also about countering migrant smuggling and, not least, addressing the root causes of migration. the approach, being tailor-made and holistic, uses all our high-level instruments and leverage to achieve our goals. in fact it represents a new methodology based on genuine partnership. the partnership addresses everything from security, return, readmission, resilience and job creation to infrastructure, investments and border management. first of all the pf approach, well received by our partners, has created a positive momentum in our dialogue with the countries in question. they do not see it either as us imposing a unilateral agenda; they do not see it as return becoming the only objective of our cooperation; and, rightly so, because the pf approach is indeed about mutually beneficial partnership and it marks a new way of engaging with our partner countries. the results we see are twofold, both in terms of better understanding european union priorities and willingness to cooperate in practice and in terms of the specific tangible outcomes as you will have seen in the report of the euco. of course we do not operate in a political vacuum and european union action must be seen as part of the bigger picture. the united nations migration-related events during the un general assembly gave high visibility and great political momentum to the migration dossier. the new york declaration for refugees and migrants, adopted at the united nations summit on 19 september 2016 by all 193 united nations member states, forms an important step in providing for a global political framework to address large movements of refugees and migrants in all aspects. we are pleased to see the notion of responsibility-sharing and the importance of international cooperation in response to migration and refugee flows reflected in the outcome. the establishment of a global compact for refugees and a global compact for safe, orderly and regular migration in the coming two years will be an important next step in moving this important agenda forward. the outcome documents closely reflect the european union priorities and policies. we reaffirm our commitment to ensuring effective implementation of the political declaration and reaffirm our engagement in the upcoming negotiation of the global compact for migration, to be concluded by 2018. the european union was able to transmit a positive narrative and show in new york that it has done more than anyone else to address migratory challenges, as well as to demonstrate its commitment towards the principle of global responsibility-sharing through the partnership framework approach, supported by the new innovative european external investment plan. we shall now capitalise on this positive momentum and continue to show a strong, united european union position also in the follow-up and the shaping of the future two global united nations compacts. all member states therein also expressed their intention to expand the number and ranges of legal powers available for refugees to be admitted to or resettled in their territory. the union resettlement framework the commission proposed could facilitate this. this is about developing a harmonised approach to resettlement at european union level, to provide safe pathways to europe for people in need of protection, replacing irregular and dangerous migrant crossings and preventing the smugglers from taking advantage of the most vulnerable. the contributions of each member state under the annual union resettlement plan will depend on member states’ contribution and engagement in the committee. we need the full support of member states on this. we also need a robust asylum system that will be able to face, not only the challenges of today, but also those in the years to come. keeping the status quo of our asylum system was not an option. the commission has put all the elements on the table to reform it. now it is time for the co-legislators to show their commitment to finding a long-term sustainable solution. the inclusion of migration in the recently adopted 2030 sustainable development agenda is therefore an important milestone. in this context the european union continues to promote a development-oriented approach towards forced displacement. we want to increase the self-reliance and resilience of refugees in their host communities with the aim of ending dependence on humanitarian aid. facilitating migration and improving migration policies, as called for in the 2013 sustainable development goals, will allow livelihoods to be improved and will enhance access for refugees to education, job markets, health and housing. as set out in the european action plan on human rights and democracy 2015-2019 and in line with the global approach to migration and mobility in the european agenda on migration, the european union and its member states are committed to enhancing human rights safeguards in all migration and mobility dialogues and cooperation frameworks with third countries and migration-related agreements, processes and programmes. in line with the european union action plan, the european union also continues to address the issue of statelessness in relations with priority countries, namely speaking out on situations of statelessness that manifest an immediate and human rights problem and supports the unhcr’s mandate and activities. migration and the fight against terrorism remain overwhelmingly the main priorities for european union action, as confirmed at the informal gac of 24-25 july this year. the updated european union syria/iraq regional strategy includes important projects in the fields of humanitarian aid, resilience and stabilisation. it calls for the respect of human rights and accountability, peace-building, gender and minority issues and condemns violations of international humanitarian law, the atrocities, killings and human rights abuses that daesh is perpetrating. within the gender action plan gap ii in european union external relations for the period 2016-2020, gender is placed at the centre of all forms of european union external relations. it commits the european union to implementing actions ensuring girls’ and women’s physical and psychological integrity, promoting their economic and social rights. together with like-minded partners, the european union will work for the elimination of all forms of violence against women, including sexual and gender-based violence in conflict and for ending impunity. all perpetrators must be brought to justice. as ms vergiat rightly pointed out, access to effective remedies for victims of migration-related human rights abuses is an issue on which further progress is still required. in this context, i would like to point out that the right to effective remedy is one of the issues dealt with in the new regulation on the european border and coast guard. this regulation respects fundamental rights and observes the principles recognised by articles 2 and 3 of the teu and reflected in the charter. in particular, it seeks to ensure full respect for human dignity, liberty and security. return of irregular migrants who do not have the right to stay in the european union to their home countries in full respect of the principle of non-refoulement is an essential part of the european union’s comprehensive efforts to address migration. in the implementation of the european union action plan on return, the european union seeks to be compliant with international human rights standards, in particular the charter of fundamental rights of the european union, the european convention for the protection of human rights and fundamental freedoms, the 1951 united nations refugee convention and its 1967 protocol. a holistic approach to migration and the cross-cutting principle of non-discrimination are the conditions for the effective respect of the human rights of migrants. our community needs to be based on integration and diversity and on the inclusion of social, cultural, linguistic and religious minorities. xenophobia, discrimination, violence and hate speech have no place. let me thank the honourable members once again for this important contribution to the debate on human rights and migration in third countries and for your excellent report.
in writing. the migration crisis is dynamic and requires flexibility and the ability to modify our policies. today, i am pleased to see a change in the original position of germany and the other western european countries, which have seen the naivety of their first fatal steps: accepting any number of migrants without criticism and pushing a programme of forced relocation of refugees to all eu countries. better late than never although poland, the czech republic or hungary should hear an apology today from those who a year ago called us egoists, who are not mature enough to be in europe. against this background, the report submitted is surprisingly outdated. the rapporteur does not distinguish between refugees and migrant workers, calls for far-reaching eu interference in the legal systems of the member states, lays out the need to create 'legal migration routes' and criticises the readmission mechanism at eu borders, calling for 'voluntary returns to be given priority over forced returns'. the rapporteur therefore calls for the eu to welcome as many migrants as it wants to bring to its territory and to provide them with social welfare, education and employment. the ecr cannot afford to be caught off guard. we express our solidarity with those forced to flee their country because of conflict, persecution or extreme poverty. however, the solutions proposed by the rapporteur to the ongoing crisis are a step backwards and show that the warning example of the calais jungle has taught some nothing.

member of the commission. – mr president, let me start by thanking this house, and in particular the rapporteur, mr gyürk, for his important work on this crucial file. the commission is fully in line with these conclusions and is ready to act upon the specific challenges highlighted in the report. as the report rightly outlines, this study can have a transformative effect on reinforcing our energy security and boosting our competitiveness by providing access to liquid hubs and a diverse range of gas sources. but before i go into some of the detail, i think it is worth recalling some of the principles which underpin our strategy. first, the diversification of the natural gas supply is a strategic objective of the european union as domestic production declines further down the road. the commission’s lng and gas storage strategy aims to exploit the potential of liquefied natural gas and gas storage to make the european union gas system more diverse and flexible, thus contributing to the key energy union objective of a secure, resilient and competitive gas supply. lng can also bring benefits in terms of competitiveness as gas markets become exposed to more competition from international suppliers. in some cases the impact can be significant, as in the case of lithuania. furthermore, lng also has the potential in some cases to reduce environmental impacts, especially in the transport sector. let me reiterate: the european union’s lng strategy was conceived with our paris climate commitments in mind. the truth is that natural gas is likely to remain an important source for our energy mix as one possible solution for a flexible energy system which includes responsive generation, demand response, grids and storage. as we work on decarbonising our economy, renewables will become more prominent in the european union’s energy mix, while gas will maintain its role with around 24-25%, pushing out other more polluting fossil fuels. that is why achieving our goals on diversity of gas supplies in every european union member state or liquid competitive markets and in meeting the needs of citizens and industry is of cardinal importance. we pursue this diversification objective on three priority axes: opening the southern gas corridor, developing an east mediterranean gas hub, and taking the opportunity provided by the positive developments of the global lng market. these axes together will considerably contribute to increased competition and a downward pressure on european gas prices. we believe that a functioning and fully-integrated liquid market is the best way to achieve our gas security objectives by making the european union attractive for suppliers and keeping prices under control through enhanced competition. that is why this strategy focuses on completing the internal gas market, both in terms of infrastructure as well as market rules, in order to provide diversification to the most vulnerable regions of the european union. now on to some of the specific points raised in the report. we welcome that mr gyürk’s report also acknowledges the importance of the established regional high-level groups in these vulnerable regions. it is only through targeted action and cooperation that we can best meet the needs of each region. these same groups are also best placed to discuss the prioritisation of infrastructure projects that can address the particular challenges. there is a successful cesec high-level group that brings together member states and energy community countries in central and south-east europe, has identified six key priority projects and already approve an action plan of regulatory solutions that we propose in our lng strategy to make them happen. the bemip high-level group is working on a similar action plan that we will deliver before the end of the year, but i could also mention the work of the south-west high level group in the iberian peninslua. on stranded assets, let me say that we are fully aware of the risks here, given today’s constantly changing environment. we need to be mindful of which infrastructure investment we follow through and should focus on only delivering those infrastructure projects that are absolutely essential to security of supply. this is also what we propose in this strategy. a limited number of key infrastructure mainly aiming at connecting to existing import terminals and a storage capacity and one lng terminal in south-east europe that will serve the whole region. here we rely on the results of existing regional cooperation. the projects put forward in the strategy have all been agreed beforehand under the three high-level groups i mentioned before. on climate and sustainability, i fully support the report’s conclusions. we need to look at both the opportunities and challenges in the lng value chain. on this point, let me stress that the commission will work closely with international partners to reduce methane slip in the overall lng chain. this is absolutely crucial to ensure that the positive aspects of using lng will not be compromised by the adverse effects of methane slip. as mentioned in the report, we should also highlight the potential of renewable sources of gas, also in the form of liquefied biogas. these sources can often utilise existing infrastructure, extending their useful lifetime further into the future. the strategy also recognises the great potential of lng in the transport sector, in particular in maritime and heavy road transport, where it can replace more polluting fuels. mr gyürk’s report also highlights the potential of small-scale lng for local industry in islands, where gas can replace oil as a fuel for power generation or feedstock. on storage, let me say that it needs to be able to compete on a level playing field. operators should be able to easily develop the more flexible products to match market needs. barriers to cross-border access should be eliminated and real cooperation on the efficient use for both business user and possibility of supply purposes should be stressed. in this regard you will be happy to hear that discussions on the gas tariff network codes have finished and the special role of lng in the european union market is well reflected in them. finally, let me turn to the international aspects rightly given prominence in the report. the study, which foresees the european union as the second largest lng importer in the world, will play a proactive role in the international efforts to promote a liquid and transparent global lng market. we will work with our international partners to promote gas trading rules that lead to more flexibility and the convergence of global gas markets. lng trade is already a subject in our energy dialogues with important consumers such as japan and current and future suppliers such as the gulf countries, the united states and canada, and this will be a step up in the future. honourable members, allow me to finish by once again by thanking the rapporteur and by stressing the importance the commission attaches to this strategy. it can have a significant impact across all five dimensions of the energy union, and i look forward to working with the european parliament to make that happen.
in writing. the european union's strategy on lng and gas storage is an important step towards improving energy security and stability. i would like to emphasise that one of the main challenges facing the european union in the framework of the common energy policy is to ensure that all citizens and economic operators have continuous and competitive access to energy, including natural gas. we have been struggling for years with the problem of gas price differentials across the eu markets. in central europe, gas prices are up to 23% higher and the market is too weakly interconnected. we cannot talk about energy security when many member states are dependent on one supplier, experiencing problems such as price discrimination or supply disruptions. the key issue to address these problems is the diversification of gas supply, including through the use of lng, as well as the development of transmission and storage infrastructure. i would like to stress that energy security depends not only on market competition but also on european union legislation and strategic agreements.
the next item is the debate on the report drawn up by mrs isabelle thomas on behalf of the committee on fisheries entitled 'how to harmonise fisheries controls in europe?' (2015/2093 (ini)) (a8-0234/2016).
in writing. – this report was drafted in preparation of the forthcoming control regulation. in brief it could be said that controls are part of the regulatory conditions under which the exploitation of the fish resources may be conducted. therefore it is important to ensure effective controls of fisheries activities in order to guarantee sustainable exploitation of living marine resources and maintain a level playing field among eu fleets. in that context member states should ensure effective implementation of the control regulation. as we know the significant improvement in the control regime has been made thanks to the current legislation in force. that not only proves that european regulations make sense but also are crucial in combating degradation of our environment. there is one point i truly want to underline: controls should not be intended as a measure where fishers are treated as criminals. the prime function of controls should be to increase compliance to agreed management measures by increasing deterrence and voluntary compliance and thus decreasing violations. a balance between enforcement and voluntary compliance should be achieved for each fishery. participatory management involving fishers and other interested parties is a key tool required by all fisheries (artisanal, small-scale and commercial) in order to ensure an increase in compliance.

the rapporteur. mr president, i would like to thank you for your kind words. ladies and gentlemen! i am very pleased, i am very pleased to be here today in the european parliament to present a report on the accessibility of central and eastern europe. i think we can all agree, as we sit here in this room, that while there is no doubt that in recent years there has been integration at the political level in the european union, this integration at the transport level still requires a great deal of effort and leaves much to be desired. this report addresses this issue and identifies the most strategic transport links - road, rail and air - that the european union and the member states on its eastern flank should build and invest in in the coming years. but one might ask, what should be the main idea of this eu project, what directions should be taken into account in particular? i think that each of you knows that studies, analyses and reports tell us that this is an increase in competitiveness, an inflow of foreign investment, an increase in security, which was also mentioned very often by the european commissioners in my talks. yes, a sense of security on the eastern flank of the european union, because a better-connected, well-organized network, a well-connected eastern europe is a safer europe. what are the main transport routes in which we will invest, we should invest in the coming years, i have taken the liberty of presenting in my report? without a doubt, ladies and gentlemen, this is the rail baltica and via baltica route, connecting the baltic countries, through poland, to southwestern europe. certainly via carpatia a project that i and many of my colleagues have been working towards for the last few years. this is a key project for the people of the eastern flank of the european union, a project that has the chance to accelerate its development, a project that has the chance to give a sense of security to the people of eastern europe, including poland, including my region of podkarpacie. the people of rzeszów, niska, stalowa wola, barwinka, krosna are waiting for this road. without this road, the equalization of development opportunities will not be possible. we will not be able to join western europe without this road, without the via carpatia. but in my report i also point out important, important river links, the road links between the elbe, the oder and the danube, between the danube and the rhine, i point out important, important, necessary in the future to invest in the trade directions: the amber route, route 11, which has every opportunity to improve the development and enhance the development, the trade exchange between poland, hungary, slovakia or slovenia. these are, ladies and gentlemen, the points that are contained in this report, which, as i said, are of a strategic nature and have a very, very, very well thought-out format, largely agreed upon by the political groups and the european commission. finally, ladies and gentlemen, i would like to thank the counter-rapporteurs, the rapporteurs from the other political groups who have worked with me on this report. i'm very pleased with this cooperation. i think that we have achieved a great result together in the form of this report, which - i repeat - has the potential to be a strategic document for the future of the european union in terms of transport development in the eastern part of the union.

in writing. there are two vectors of eu security to look at: both internal and external. the most important problem in the internal dimension is the crisis of successive waves of refugees and terrorist attacks. both of these issues are strongly linked to the issues of foreign security around the eu's borders. these are, without a doubt, the issues that have been fatal in the arab spring and the decision of the french, british and italian governments to support the rebels. another factor of equal importance is the hybrid war that russia has waged against the west. i am not just thinking about ukraine, but also about cyber attacks and disinformation directed towards central and eastern european countries, including my homeland poland. so far, the eu institutions have failed to find a solution to any of these threats - and well, because such solutions are only created within the member states. security was, is and will be the inherent domain of sovereign states. contrary to the dreams of the communists, the euro-socialists and the fanatics of european federation, there is no common security policy.

in writing. ‒ i support the draft legislative resolution of the european parliament on the draft council implementing decision on the launch in denmark of the automated data exchange for 2016 fingerprint data. cross-border cooperation in the exchange of data is a necessary element for ensuring security and combating terrorism and cross-border crime. in particular, in the context of the large influx of undocumented and unverified persons into europe, and the presence of tens of thousands of persons without right of residence, and thus without access to support systems and legal functioning in the market, exposing them to the influence of the criminal world, it is necessary to develop cooperation on data exchange. responsible and effective control is necessary to ensure that member states adopt adequate security policies and to safeguard one of europe's most important values, the free movement of persons and cultural diversity.
