mr. chairman, please! once again, the old adage that temporary solutions are the most permanent has been proven true. it will soon be a quarter of a century since the transitional vat system came into force in the single market. everyone was aware that he was imperfect, susceptible to fraud and manipulation. the commission then committed itself to prepare final, improved regulations quickly, but only now announces that it intends to propose such a draft by 2017. the assumptions put forward by the commission indicate that it has adopted minimalistic objectives. this is not surprising, however, given that this legal act must be agreed by all member states. the vat gap in some member states is close to 40%. this situation needs to be improved quickly, and it would be good to look at the solutions used in some member states and discuss them. one solution is to adopt a so-called reverse vat, i.e. the principle that the consumer of the product and service would be the payer. this solution allows for the partial closure of many loopholes and makes it difficult to circumvent the law. at least that is the conclusion of countries that have partially implemented such a system. the union and its member states cannot afford such huge tax losses, especially in a period of budgetary stability problems and rising public expenditure. i therefore wish the commission good luck and perseverance on this subject and that is why i voted in favour of the report.
in writing. ‒ i voted against the reform of the european vat system, because of concerns about the possibility of interfering with competences that are the exclusive competence of the member states. i do not think that the current taxation rules should be harmonised. the european union may apply general guidance to the member states in this respect. tax legislation is the exclusive competence of the member states and it is for the member states to organise the rates and the collection of vat in practice. due to concerns about interference in the internal affairs of the state in this matter, i voted against.
in writing. ‒ the purpose of this report is to discuss the commission's work on reforming the european vat system and combating vat fraud across europe. the possible directions of reform are set out in more detail in the commission's action plan on vat, which was published last spring. the european parliament expects the commission to present a proposal on the definitive vat system by 2017. however, the report contains many provisions aimed at harmonising tax policies between eu member states. i also do not support the inclusion of financial services in vat and the creation of another body that would be an independent european public prosecutor's office. i have hereby disapproved the report.
in writing. ‒ the vat system in the european union, which has existed since 1993, was introduced as a transitional solution. it was to be replaced by definitive rules based, in principle, on the taxation of supplies of goods and services in the member state of destination. unfortunately, after 23 years, the system remains unchanged, contributing to a widening vat gap and significant cross-border fraud. in 2016, the european commission finally decided to submit a legislative proposal to base the vat system on the principle of taxation in the country of destination of goods and services, rather than the country of origin as it has been the case until now. the commission also announced that it would present a proposal to modernise and simplify the vat system for cross-border e-commerce. the main thrust of the solution is to introduce a one-stop shop for online sales of tangible goods to final consumers and to abolish the vat exemption for imports of small consignments of goods from third country suppliers. i believe that the commission's proposal is a step in the right direction, that it will facilitate cross-border activities and help to close the current vat gap. at the same time, i am pleased that the european parliament document clearly emphasises that the member states remain independent in setting the standard rate and the reduced rate of vat.
in writing. ‒ the purpose of this report is to discuss the commission's work on reforming the european vat system and combating vat fraud across europe. unfortunately, the direction taken does not guarantee effective action against vat fraud, causing more chaos in the institutions responsible for the vat system. at the same time, it should be added that member states should make use of the available means to combat vat fraud in a measurable way. that's why i voted against the resolution.
in writing. ‒ i voted in favour of the european union action plan against illegal wildlife trade. the adopted plan aims to combat and prevent crime linked to illicit trafficking within the eu. i believe that action should be taken to combat these practices effectively. to this end, better coordination of cooperation and more effective prevention systems should be established. there is also a need to build comprehensive and coordinated action by member states in different policy areas. the issue of strengthening the eu rules governing the importation into the member states of objects protected by eu regulations is also an important one. i voted in favour of the regulation, seeing that it was necessary to regulate these matters.
in writing. ‒ i voted in favour of the report on the eu action plan against illegal wildlife trade. wildlife trafficking is a multi-billion euro criminal business dominated by organised crime groups that, motivated by high profits and low risks, have for years destroyed, often irreversibly, valuable species of flora and fauna. the european parliament's action plan, built around three priorities: preventing and addressing wildlife trafficking, ensuring effective implementation and enforcement of existing legislation to combat organised wildlife crime, and deepening global partnerships with countries of origin, transit and destination to combat illegal wildlife trafficking, is, in my view, essential for the protection of nature and the natural heritage of europe and the world.
in writing. ‒ in recent years, the world has seen an increase in wildlife crime. shocking images of rhinos and elephants bleeding to death, and of birds, amphibians, and reptiles being smuggled across borders and held in inhumane conditions, have become commonplace. moreover, the illegal trade in wildlife has become one of the most lucrative activities of organised crime groups, with an estimated turnover of between eur 8 billion and eur 20 billion per year. in recent years, there has also been a significant increase in the global demand for animals themselves or their products, and the scale of trade is now so large that many of the most recognizable species on earth are now threatened. one factor that facilitates the illegal trade in wildlife is the heterogeneity of legal systems across countries, which leads to international organised crime moving with the sale to countries with low sanctions or low effectiveness of the relevant services. combating this practice therefore requires a closer partnership between the countries of origin and transit and the countries of destination, as well as cooperation between regional actors. without this, i fear we will soon see the extinction of many precious species of plants and animals in various parts of the world.

in writing. ‒ small and medium-sized transport enterprises play a key role in ensuring proper mobility in europe, but often face significant difficulties in gaining access to or maintaining their market presence, mainly due to existing monopolies. by having a better knowledge of the local market, closer contact with the customer or, more often, flexibility and the ability to innovate, small businesses improve individual passenger transport, especially in the difficult final leg of journeys in densely populated or highly isolated areas. that's why their support is so important. particular attention should therefore be paid to further reducing existing bureaucratic obstacles or combating monopolies, as well as to technological support and the development of the sharing economy for smes. it is necessary to promote convergence between the traditional economy and new platforms that support innovation in smes. to achieve this, a more transnational, european approach to the cooperative business model needs to be developed.

deputising for the author. – mr president, having electricity at home, at work, and virtually everywhere, is so obvious that we rarely give this any thought, but more than a billion people live without electricity and still more only have unreliable access. this is but one aspect of the shocking gap between living conditions in our world, but it has a number of consequences for people’s health and safety, education, well—being and chance to earn a living; for women who carry out the difficult, time—consuming and sometimes risky task of collecting firewood and have to use unhealthy and hazardous cooking methods; for the development progress – or lack thereof – of communities and countries; for the preservation of vegetation, forest and biodiversity; for local climates and for the global effort to limit climate change and handle its consequences; and of course sometimes also for peace and security, as the energy issue can spawn conflict. access to energy is a key driver of development. ensuring access to affordable, reliable, sustainable and modern energy for all is one of the sdgs adopted in the united nations last year. this goal should be achieved by 2030. getting there will take truly huge efforts but it is possible and necessary. how, then, should it be done? what is the eu’s contribution and what progress is being achieved with this contribution? these are the core issues of the oral question to the commission and the motion for a resolution prepared by the committee on development. our parliament has been emphasising for years that the focus should be on the small-scale production of renewable energy, local networks and off—grid solutions. such solutions produce the biggest contribution to development and are best at avoiding negative impacts on the environment. we have also seen that the regulation on the development cooperation instrument prescribes this orientation of eu development policy in the energy area. not least, we note in our scrutiny of the draft development assistance programming documents that the prescription is being followed. the potential for renewable energy production is particularly great in africa, which is also where electrification is least developed. solar and wind power generation should be expanded faster. insufficient and hazardous traditional use of biomass, such as firewood and charcoal, currently dominates africa’s energy consumption. a cautious approach to more modern types of bioenergy is necessary since such energy production can come at the cost of food production, affect land use rights, cause deforestation and degradation of land and reduce the availability of water for other purposes. energy poverty is most widespread in rural areas, but providing access to energy in rapidly growing cities is also a massive challenge. the unsatisfied needs are particularly extensive in africa. in fact, the number of people without electricity on this continent is increasing, while population growth is faster than the progress of electrification. climate finance provided by developed to developing countries is another important source. together with technology transfer, it also affects africa leaders’ wish to focus on renewable energy sources and industrialisation processes. in parallel with public funds, more private money must go into energy investment. public-private partnerships can be useful and the general trend in eu development policy towards providing grants, loans, subsidies and other incentives for private investment is particularly strong in the area of energy investment. the eu has recently launched an electrification financing initiative, electrifi and facilitating energy investment is also among the central aims of the european external investment plan proposed by the commission. development effectiveness principles should always be followed. the eu can be proud of the scale of its work to extend energy provision in developing countries. in the period 2014—2020 we are spending eur 3.5 billion on development assistance in the energy area. the commission proposal for a new european consensus on development rightly points to the crucial role of energy for development and in climate action. in 2012 the commission set out to provide access to sustainable energy for an additional 500 million people in developing countries by 2030. we are now asking the commission to tell us about the general state of progress, the main challenges encountered and the outlook for the continued implementation of development assistance in the energy area. we would also like to know what proportion of the funds engaged is going to local renewable energy projects and how we can achieve the target of eur 500 billion. i look forward to listening to the commission’s reply.

in writing. ‒ through the eu solidarity fund (eusf), the european union is providing effective support to member states or eu candidate countries in their response to natural disasters. we allocate up to eur 500 million per year from this fund to supplement public expenditure incurred by the state or member states in connection with emergency operations. the eusf shall provide assistance where the total direct damage caused by a natural disaster exceeds eur 3 billion or 0,6% of the gross national income of the country concerned. the evaluation report on the european union solidarity fund adopted this week highlights the need for rapid intervention by the eusf, the need for a policy of prevention of overlapping with other european instruments, especially cohesion policy, and for effective cooperation at national level with regional or local authorities. in this context, given that the speed of processing applications in the event of natural disasters is of the utmost importance, the rapporteur has rightly proposed a timeframe not exceeding 12 weeks from the submission of the complete dossier . in addition, it is proposed to introduce greater transparency, in particular as regards the various resources allocated to the compensation of damage caused by such a disaster.
in writing. ‒ following the tragic floods in 2002, the european union established the european union solidarity fund (regulation (ec) no 2012/2002). it is a direct expression of the union's solidarity with countries affected by major natural disasters. it is intended not only for the member states but also for the countries applying for eu membership. in 2014, the original regulation was amended to respond more effectively to the concerns of beneficiaries and to expedite the processing of applications from disaster-affected countries and to include drought in the list of regulated disasters (regulation (eu) no 661/2014). in october 2015, the european commission presented a report on the use of the european union solidarity fund (eusf) for 2014. the 'collective regulation' proposed by the commission on 14 september provides for a new revision of the fund to improve the speed and efficiency of the system for financing emergency operations. i hereby endorse the report.
in writing. ‒ the european union solidarity fund was established in response to the catastrophic floods that occurred in central europe in the summer of 2012. this instrument enables the union to respond to major natural disasters and exceptional regional disasters within the community and in countries negotiating accession to the community. in 2014, the fund underwent a major reform to streamline and simplify procedures and ensure a faster response to a disaster, even within 6 weeks of the application. unfortunately, since the creation of the fund, the frequency of natural disasters has increased significantly, with serious consequences for societies. i therefore believe that this instrument should be considerably strengthened in the coming years. it is also necessary to further simplify the procedure for receiving advances and paying the final amount, as well as to ensure the greatest possible transparency in the allocation, management and implementation of the fund. the eu solidarity fund debate is also a good opportunity to recall the member states' obligation to invest in disaster prevention. such actions may be financed, inter alia, under the structural funds.
in writing. ‒ in principle, member states should act in solidarity to deal with natural disasters worldwide. it is important that aid is effectively directed both to member states and to countries that inspire confidence in the proper use of funds. another important issue is the amount of aid. for eu policy to be effective, the amount of aid to the countries that need it most and are entitled to it should be increased. the report adopted in this version raises the concern that these issues will not be properly organised, which is why i voted against the report.
in writing. ‒ the european union solidary fund (eusf) has mobilised in total eur 3.8 billion in connection with more than 70 disasters. against this background, disasters in romania and france, which caused serious damages in 2014, were considered to be illegible for eusf funding. this why the new regulation from 2014 made some clarification of the rules on the eligibility of regional natural disasters setting a threshold at 1.5% of regional gdp together with the possibility of making advance payments of up to 10% of the likely amount of aid. in addition, a six-week deadline by which the commission must respond to applications has been introduced. nevertheless, i agree with rapporteur that if we really want to stop victims feeling abandoned between emergency intervention and the arrival of eusf funds, further reforms are needed. therefore, we should increase the advance payments threshold from 10 to 15%, shorten the deadlines for processing the applications from six weeks to four weeks and allow for a single application to be submitted jointly by several eligible states at cross-border level. taking the above into account, i voted in favour of this report.
in writing. ‒ i voted in favour of the report on the european union solidarity fund because i agree with the positive assessment of its functioning. the fund is one of the most concrete and measurable forms of support that the european union can provide to local communities in the event of disasters and natural disasters. in addition to addressing the consequences of these phenomena, the fund should also be used for preventive purposes, which will allow the losses incurred to be minimised. it is also necessary to fully control and improve the transparency of the use of the fund's resources. the court of auditors, whose audits have so far revealed irregularities, has an important role to play in this respect, but so do the member states, whose final accounts of the use made of the aid received should be made public and generally available. i voted in favour of the resolution because it not only confirms the many advantages of the functioning of the fund but also points out the issues which, if resolved, will improve its effectiveness.
in writing. ‒ i voted in favour of the agreement between the united states of america and the eu on the protection of personal information relating to the prevention, detection, investigation and prosecution of criminal offences. i believe that the provisions of the agreement contribute to building a security system, strengthening the detection and deterrence of crime and facilitating investigations. the agreement facilitates the prevention of terrorist activities by the relevant authorities. the important aspect here is that the contract itself does not provide a legal basis for the transfer of personal data, but only adds a layer of privacy protection to personal data transferred under other contracts. the agreement also contains provisions on procedures to be followed in the event of interference with basic data. i think this deal will help increase security.
in writing. ‒ this agreement provides for additional protection of personal data transferred and processed for the purposes of preventing, investigating, detecting or prosecuting criminal offences, including terrorism. the contract itself does not constitute a legal basis for the transfer of personal data, but only enhances the privacy protection of personal data transferred under other contracts. this agreement contains provisions setting out several basic data protection principles, namely the purpose and limitations of use, the quality and integrity of data, provisions on onward transfer, provisions on collective transfer and the right to legal redress. the united states has also provided the united states with a number of other legal instruments to facilitate the enforcement of the law. the agreement represents a significant step forward in the protection of personal data transferred between the eu and the us, without hampering the work of law enforcement and intelligence agencies. it will be subject to regular monitoring and review, the results of which will be made publicly available. i hereby endorse the report.
in writing. ‒ the decision to sign a data protection agreement between the us and the eu is a very important step towards ensuring the comprehensive protection of our data, while respecting high privacy standards. the agreement with the united states covers all transfers of data such as names, addresses or criminal records. the transfer of such information shall be aimed at supporting the fight against transnational crime, including the prevention, detection, investigation and prosecution of cross-border crime, including terrorism. until now, such data have been transferred to us law enforcement authorities on the basis of bilateral agreements between the eu member states and the us. but they were not protected. with the agreement, this situation will be completely changed. data transferred to the us for the purpose of fighting crime will be protected in the same way as in europe. the same appeal procedures and control procedures as in the union will also apply. the agreement does not cover the exchange of data between national safety authorities, as such exchange is not within the competence of the union. nor does it cover transatlantic data transfers between private entities.
in writing. ‒ this agreement provides for additional protection of personal data transferred and processed for the purposes of preventing, investigating, detecting or prosecuting criminal offences, including terrorism. it contains provisions setting out several basic data protection principles, including data transfer rules, rules on transfers and the right of an entity to legal redress. the agreement represents a significant step forward in the protection of personal data transferred between the eu and the us, without hampering the work of law enforcement and intelligence agencies. that's why i voted for the deal.

in writing. ‒ i voted against the report on liability, compensation and financial security for offshore oil and gas activities, because of my many doubts. i do not think that the proposed extension of the scope of the rules is necessary. the existing provisions on the subject matter do not require the proposed amendments. the regulation of these matters is sufficient to safeguard the safety of offshore fuel extraction activities.
in writing. ‒ more than 90% of oil and 60% of gas produced in europe comes from offshore activities. such exploration and production activities are already being carried out or planned in the territorial seas of 18 eu member states. consequently, it was necessary to introduce provisions to protect against losses caused by such activities at sea. the new rules were adopted by the european parliament at its november plenary session in brussels. the effectiveness of national schemes in relation to pollution damage caused by such activities is based on systems for dealing with claims for compensation and the availability of financial security instruments. at present, with the exception of france, the netherlands and denmark, in many member states there is little likelihood of the complainants obtaining compensation, especially where they are indirectly injured enterprises such as fish processing plants. in this context, the european commission should work closely with member states to ensure that compensation and financial security systems for activities related to oil and natural gas deposits in eu offshore areas are adapted to current requirements. they must provide compensation for claims by third parties and for traditional damage caused by failures in such maritime activities.
in writing. ‒ the report strongly calls for increased liability for offshore oil and gas deposits. it calls for a eu liability framework in this area, calling for harmonisation of minimum liability for civil damages and recommending a common eu-level mechanism for handling incidents (another agency). the commission is also invited to consider the creation of a legal compensation mechanism and it is proposed to extend its scope to secondary damage (paragraph 3). it also calls on the commission to add major accidents in the oil extraction sector to the environmental offences directive, regretting that the definitions of offences in this area have not been harmonised. equally importantly, the commission is invited to consider a proposal to establish a fund to be set up from fees paid by the offshore mining sector. however, the amendments on minimum interference in national policy were ignored.
in writing. ‒ following the deepwater horizon oil spill and explosion, a directive on the safety of offshore oil and gas operations was adopted. it aims to establish minimum requirements for the prevention of major accidents in this type of activity and to limit the consequences of such accidents. the directive provides that concessionaires are absolutely responsible for preventing and remedying environmental damage caused by their activities. however, the directive does not regulate civil liability for damage caused to natural or legal persons. nor does it establish criminal liability for accidents in maritime areas. the european commission should therefore work more closely with the member states to ensure that compensation and financial security schemes for offshore oil and gas activities in the eu allow for the swift and proper handling of claims. it is equally important to provide a legal framework for actions to repair environmental damage caused by a marine casualty in accordance with the 'polluter pays' principle.

in writing. ‒ i voted in favour of the report on the application of the european order for payment procedure. i believe that the scope of the regulation in this area will facilitate recovery in cross-border cases. the procedure is voluntary, which means that it is available in cross-border cases as an alternative to the various equivalent national procedures. in summary, this procedure allows creditors to obtain an order for the recovery of undisputed civil and commercial claims easily. such an order may be requested by letter or, often, by electronic means, does not require the assistance of a lawyer and is enforceable in other member states without any further formalities. it should be noted that the current regulations in force in the member states in this field are very effective.
in writing. ‒ the purpose of the european order for payment procedure is to facilitate the recovery of sums in cross-border cases. the procedure allows creditors to obtain an order for the recovery of undisputed civil and commercial claims easily. such an order may be requested by letter or, often, by electronic means, does not require the assistance of a lawyer and is enforceable in other member states without any further formalities. the european order for payment is issued automatically, solely on the basis of an action, but the debtor may lodge an objection within 30 days. i hereby endorse the report.
in writing. ‒ the european order for payment procedure is designed to enable the recovery of debts that are certain, of a fixed amount, due and uncontested by the defendant, in a rapid, easy and inexpensive manner. it should be borne in mind that late payments are the main cause of bankruptcy. this threatens the existence of enterprises, especially small and medium-sized enterprises, and leads to the loss of many jobs. however, i am concerned that there are significant differences between member states in the application of the european order for payment procedure. difficulties also arise in the acceptance of applications in other european languages, which negatively affects the costs and time of the proceedings. in this context, it is therefore of the utmost importance to take practical steps to further simplify the existing procedures and to inform citizens and businesses about the availability, functioning, application and benefits of the european order for payment procedure in cross-border cases.

also critical for developing short-sea shipping as an alternative to road transport as part of our strategy to decarbonise transport. this is why maritime ports are extremely valuable assets to be preserved and strengthened. that is what we will achieve with the regulation discussed today, and that is why the commission considers this file a priority under the work programme for 2016. first, the regulation will ensure greater transparency for the use of public funds in ports. many receive considerable financial support from both national and eu budgets. transparency will contribute to a genuine level playing field between european ports. it will also help to make public funding more efficient. the court of auditors stressed the need to address this issue in a recent report. second, the regulation creates a common framework for the provision of port services. this framework brings legal stability for the tendering of port services. it will end today’s unclear situation where port policy is not decided by you, the legislators, but rather by judgments of the european court of justice on a case-by-case basis. third, it will ensure better training of port workers in line with the work undertaken by the social partners. finally, the regulation will contribute to our decarbonisation strategy. we need to green the shipping industry and promote short-sea shipping. this requires investment and the right type of investment in ports, and investments need transparency. many of you attach great importance to clear and simple state aid rules. the commission shares this attachment. we have been working a lot on the issue of state aid in ports over the last months. my colleague, commissioner vestager, and i are making sure that the views of european ports are adequately taken into account. replying last week to a parliamentary question from mr fleckenstein the commission clarified the framework for state aid in ports, including the general block exemption regulation. the situation is as follows. a new set of infrastructure analytical grids was published on 2 december 2016. with this document, the commission explains which infrastructures are considered to be non—economic and which should therefore not fall under the state aid rules. this infrastructure includes defence infrastructure, such as dykes, and access infrastructure to ports, such as a river flowing through the port that can be used by anyone. last week, the commission also completed its second public consultation on the general block exemption regulation. its objective is to identify which public investments in port infrastructure are considered state aid, but which are unproblematic and therefore do not need to be notified. we are now analysing the replies to improve the text further and adopt the regulation in 2017. the result of the analytical grid and a revised general block exemption regulation will be more legal certainty and more clarity. but there will be no change in the decision-making practice of the commission. with this work we are doing exactly what you have been calling for under recital 45 of the port services regulation. however, for institutional reasons and to recall the better law-making principles agreed between the commission and the co-legislators, we will record a statement from the commission regarding this recital. the text is balanced. it is the result of three years of discussion with all the stakeholders. all major organisations representing the european port sector stand behind it; the trade unions, port authorities, port terminal operators and port service providers. it received a strong support in the transport committee and was accepted unanimously by member states. so now it is time to conclude the legislative procedure in first reading. all the circumstances allow it.

vice-president of the commission. – madam president, distinguished members, as you will remember, on the previous occasions when we have met over the past two years i was always telling you about our plans, objectives and our future path for creating the energy union, one which serves europe’s citizens, boosts our industries and preserves our environment. but at this point in time as we are meeting in december 2016, i would like to say to you that our internal work in the commission is now almost entirely complete. we have presented to you over the past two years the strategy, the legislation and the enabling environment for turning the energy union from a catchy buzzword to the reality we live in. with last week’s package we are 90% done with what we have promised, and now we very much need the european parliament to make sure that the energy union also becomes a legal reality. we need to work together to make sure that we start the co-legislative process as early as possible. of course, last week’s package was rather a big one. it has eight legislative proposals and some important political communications and reports, so i shall just focus on the three main goals: how to put energy efficiency first; how to achieve global leadership in renewables; and what we can do to provide a really fair deal for our consumers. as you will have already noticed, this package is bound to have a huge impact on jobs and growth. it could generate around a 1% increase in gdp in the next 10 years. it could spur investment of eur 177 billion and it would directly improve the life and quality of our citizens. on this last aspect it was very important for us to have a particular social component in the package, particularly for those who have difficulties in paying their energy bills, and to make sure that the transition we are starting will be a transition which we can call socially fair. as you can imagine, because of the time constraints i will not be able to go into the details of the overall package, so i will just focus on some elements of the new governance systems we are proposing. when we discussed it the last time, in december 2015, you were very much inviting the commission to present a legislative proposal on the governance. we listened very carefully to you and we proposed such a proposal. it serves three objectives. first, it streamlines the different planning and reporting obligations, and we are making sure that we will really get rid of overlapping reporting obligations, we will align the reporting in terms of frequency and timing, and i believe that what we are putting on the table is in full accordance with the reporting and planning of the paris agreement. so it will allow us to continue to play a leading role in the paris agreement implementation. secondly, you have been very much calling for increased transparency and more predictability, which we introduced into the system as well because we see them as two essential conditions to attract investments and indeed to fundamentally transform and modernise our economies. thirdly, we are proposing a mechanism that is solid and robust so we can collectively reach all the energy union’s objectives, in particular the 2030 targets, and to put europe firmly on the road to a low-carbon economy and society. how do we want to achieve it? the key instrument will be the national energy and climate plans, plans that have a long-term perspective of 2030 or even 2050. the plans will cover all five dimensions of the energy union and will be the result of consultations with other neighbouring member states because we know how important regional cooperation in this aspect is. we would like to make sure that the work on these plans will start swiftly because we would like to see the final form by the beginning of 2019, and this will be an important goal of my second energy union which i would like to start in february next year and where i hope some of you, as we did the last time, could join me. then we will have a system of biannual reports and every year we will also issue a report on the energy union, where we will analyse the overall situation in europe and where we will also if needed issue the necessary recommendations. i see that time is flying by. therefore, madam president, i would like to pass the floor, if you will allow, also to commissioner arias cañete so that he can go into more detail on the concrete legislative proposals.
member of the commission. – madam president, as explained by vice-president šefčovič, the main building blocks of the legislative proposals cover energy efficiency, renewable energy, the design of the electricity market and governance rules for the energy union. let me start with energy efficiency first. we are proposing, as we promised, a european union binding target of 30% for 2030, up from the current target of at least 27%. a 30% target is the most cost-effective option by 2030. it will create about 400 000 more new jobs, reduce gas imports by 12% and save eur 70 billion in fossil fuel import bills. for buildings, a sector which accounts for 40% of europe’s energy consumption, we are proposing to speed up the renovation rate and promote the use of innovative and smart technologies. this will boost activity and revive employment in the construction and engineering sectors. as examples of concrete measures we propose prolonging the savings obligations in order to contribute to the energy efficiency target, deploying about five million electric vehicle recharging points, and encouraging greater use of renewable energy in buildings, which is currently just 16%. with this set of measures, our proposal will speed up investment in the renovation of buildings, create a building renovation market with a value between eur 80 and 120 billion in 2030, lower energy bills for consumers, and take up to 3.2 million households out of energy poverty. last, but not least: for products, the commission has adopted a new ecodesign working plan. on renewable energy, our aim is to be world leaders, maximising the use of renewable energy in buildings, transport and industry. our new rules will ensure that the renewable energy target of at least 27% by 2030 is reached. first, we are putting the investment framework right by consolidating several core principles for support for renewable energy in european union legislation. we move away from national schemes and propose a progressive europeanisation through cross-border opening of support. we want to put an end to retroactive changes in support, and we call for simplified administrative procedures to get the projects up and running. second, we propose measures for the sectors which have the highest potential for the deployment of renewable energy: transport, heating and cooling, and electricity. in transport the proposed measures will boost the use of advanced biofuels, electricity and renewable synthetic fuels. we have proposed an ambitious mandate of 6.8% by 2030, with a strong component of 3.6% of advanced biofuels. on bioenergy in particular, after many years of uncertainty, we are introducing strengthened sustainability criteria for biomass. also, in line with our earlier position, we propose to progressively reduce the contribution of food-based biofuels to meet the european union’s renewable target: from 7% in 2021 to 3.8% by 2030. this is both realistic and proportionate. the renewables directive also includes a number of options for member states to increase their share of renewable energy in heating and cooling supply by one percentage point per year until 2030. furthermore, our proposal opens access rights to local district heating and cooling systems for producers of renewable heating and cooling and waste from industry, and third parties acting on their behalf. this takes me to the third area: renewable electricity. our target of at least 27% also means a 50% share of renewables in our electricity mix. here the proposed renewables directive and the new market design proposals work hand in hand. we are overhauling the electricity market, and we do so mainly in two ways. first, by changing the rules of the market. the new market rules will promote a more flexible market. sharper price signals will prompt investment in demand response, storage and quickly reacting generation. our proposals will make trading easier by better integrating short-term markets. second, by fostering regional cooperation. we will create regional operational centres where transmission system operators will cooperate to ensure optimal use of the european electricity grid and better security of supply. and we will set up a europe-wide dso entity to coordinate the operation and planning of the transmission and distribution networks. third, by giving a european dimension to security of supply. we will develop common rules on crisis prevention and tools to ensure cross-border cooperation to confront new threats to security of supply, such as cyber-attacks. and we will establish a common framework for capacity remuneration mechanisms. this framework will build on a wider european adequacy assessment. all available capacities, including in neighbouring states, will be taken into account and this will make sure that the right amount of capacity is identified. we provide rules the rules to ensure cross-border participation. this is a big change compared with today, and it will keep costs to consumers to a minimum and preserve the functioning of the internal market. but i want to be very clear on one more point. capacity mechanisms will not be used as a backdoor subsidy for high-polluting fossil fuels. that would go against our climate objectives. that is why we have set a limit of 550 grams of carbon dioxide per kilowatt-hour for new plants, and existing capacity mechanisms also have to adapt to the new rules in due time. in all of this, our european union agency for the cooperation of energy regulators (acer) will ensure the proper regulatory oversight. we propose therefore to reinforce acer’s powers to meet these tasks. finally, allow me to underline one of the essential elements of the package, namely putting consumers at the centre. the new rules will enable them not only to be more informed or to change their provider more easily, but to be able, if they want, to produce their own renewable electricity and be paid for electricity they feed into the grid. in that case, their contribution to the grid costs should be fair and cost-reflective while they continue to benefit from facilitated access to the market – the so-called priority dispatch. i expect this complete set of proposals will be adopted by the co-legislators as quickly as possible.

in writing. ‒ i voted in favour of the report on the eu's coherent policy for the cultural and creative sectors. there is no doubt that the cultural and creative industries are a particularly strong part of the european economy, and are europe's business card and identity in the world. they have a huge potential both to foster the european union's economic growth, innovation and competitiveness, but also to promote and nurture our tradition and cultural diversity. there is no doubt that they need special support to enable them to develop without restriction, and i therefore agree with the rapporteurs that it is necessary to develop an industrial strategy at european level which takes account of the specific characteristics of these industries and meets their needs, for example in the field of copyright or digitisation. furthermore, i would like to point out that many of the companies in this sector are family businesses and, due to their particular legal situation, require a comprehensive approach, especially in relation to issues such as inheritance law.
in writing. ‒ i supported this report because the cultural and creative sectors are extremely important to the european economy. suffice it to say that they are made up of 3 million enterprises employing 12 million workers. the importance of this sector is also due to the fact that it is difficult to transfer existing jobs to other countries and continents. firstly, because they are linked to specific cultural competences and social experience. in addition, young people and women, the groups most affected by unemployment, are more likely to find employment in these sectors. if we look at the structure of young people's education, they very often take up education in these areas, which means that we have adequate human resources within the union. the lack of an eu strategy for this sector of the economy is therefore surprising. this means that not only is there no vision of how to exploit the existing potential, but above all we are not thinking about how to use the eu instruments and programmes to strengthen the industry in question and thus create new and stable jobs. the best example of the failure of this sector is the fact that no funding has been allocated to projects in these sectors so far under the european fund for strategic investments, one of whose priorities is to support the cultural and creative sectors.

in writing. ‒ cultural and creative industries are based on cultural values, individual creativity and skills and talents that can generate income and create jobs by generating profits. the cultural and creative sectors employ more than 12 million people (employing 7.5% of the total workforce). their value in terms of sales of goods and services is eur 509 billion (5.3% of total gross value added in europe). in the 21st century europe, marked by the transformation to the digital economy, cultural and creative industries are increasingly replacing traditional production processes and value chains. the report focuses on, inter alia, the definition of social and economic value, impact, potential and the challenges facing the cultural and creative sectors today. i hereby endorse the report.
in writing. ‒ the cultural and creative industries have the potential to contribute to alleviating the current economic and employment challenges in the european union and to promoting sustainable growth that is conducive to social inclusion and innovation. to achieve this, it is necessary to develop a comprehensive, coherent and long-term industrial policy framework for the creative and cultural sectors, in order to ensure that they are adequately funded, increase their competitiveness and enable them to realise their potential for creating high-quality jobs and growth. in this context, it is worth mentioning the need to raise awareness, especially among young people, of the possibilities of developing careers in craft and production occupations linked to the cultural and creative sectors. finally, it is essential to improve the investment environment and to broaden the range of financial instruments available to businesses, while promoting mixed financing, in particular in the form of public-private partnerships. this is particularly important for small and medium-sized enterprises.
in writing. ‒ i welcome the joint report by itre and cult on a coherent eu policy for the cultural and creative sectors. it is our next step in raising awareness of the crucial role these sectors play in the eu's social and economic development. the report properly defines the potential for generating growth and jobs in the cultural and creative industries, while highlighting their significant impact in areas such as new business models, creativity and innovation, and digitalisation and skills development. the report also places particular emphasis on building high-quality sectoral data sources that will allow better policy-making in the future, support innovation and training, and ensure adequate funding under eu programmes to support cultural and creative industries. in line with the recommendations outlined in the report, i consider it necessary to define specific indicators to monitor and analyse the cultural, economic and social impact of the cultural and creative sectors. in this context, i also consider it desirable to explore and identify alternative sources of data to complement and improve official statistics, given that the cultural and creative industries often use complex business models that can challenge traditional forms of analysis and funding.

mr. chairman, please! fellow workers! one remark and one controversy. i am very pleased that the report focuses on the key issues: religious freedom, protesting against persecuted christians, protecting the rights of refugees and combating human trafficking. it's a true barbaric plague of the modern world. but the report, and above all our discussion, should avoid bias and here again a polemic with mr lambsdorff, who did not answer my question and that of mr jurko. in poland, which you so freely criticize, there is very strong protection for national minorities: germans in poland have full schooling rights, their own schools, education, and even parliamentary representation. germany, on the other hand, does not fully recognise the rights of national minorities. so i invite you to poland to see the good examples that your country and europe could use.
in writing. as we do every year, we discuss the state of human rights in the world. at the same time, we rarely see the union itself contributing to their violation outside its territory. this is the case for private military and security companies from its territory. some eu member states are among the largest exporters of military and security services. these entities operate in a grey area of responsibility. the eu has excluded them from the provisions of the services directive and its representatives are quite arrogantly opposing the development of an international convention at the un that would introduce legal regulations and restrictions on their activities. the argument that existing soft law instruments, i.e. those which are not legally binding, such as the montreux document or the code of conduct for private security providers, are sufficient is not only ridiculous but already compromises the eu on the international stage. the european external action service has an unflattering role to play in this respect. i therefore expect the high representative of the union for foreign affairs and security policy to revise this position so that eu actors do not violate human rights outside the eu and the eu does not block the adoption of international regulations that aim to bring private military and security companies into the international legal framework.
madam president! the future of european cooperation depends on the mutual and solidarity-based partnership of our countries, but also on respect for the peoples of europe. the report contains very important statements, for example on the significance and sad prospects of the involvement of thousands of young european muslims in the forces of the islamic state's caliphate, or on the growing russian expansion in eastern europe. but the conclusions are fatally stereotypical: more power for the integrated eu institutions, but unfortunately this fatal tone of disregard, aggression, exclusion towards europeans who remain in opposition, in legitimate opposition to the authorities of the european union or to the governments that support them. ladies and gentlemen, one thing is certain: the sooner the european establishment learns to respect the millions of europeans who disagree with its policies, the more bad news we will avoid in the future.
in writing. the situation around the european union is changing for the worse. large areas of north africa and the middle east are engulfed in war, and terrorist groups are increasingly infiltrating europe. other threats are emerging, such as the war in eastern ukraine and cyber attacks. we must therefore increase the eu's responsibility for our common security. i know there is no chance of creating a common european army, but we can take action in the eu that would improve our security more effectively. i see three such pragmatic ventures. first, a joint permanent headquarters for civil-military operations should be established in the european union. secondly, the union must respond more quickly to threats by using its own battle groups for joint missions and operations. finally, thirdly, a separate fund should be created within the eu to finance the common security and defence policy. i believe that these actions would increase the defence and security capacity of the european union.

member of the commission. – madam president, i thank all the people that responded to this very important debate. as you know, the common agricultural policy that was agreed in 2013 by the co-legislators reiterated in support of the market orientation of that policy. this is what the council and the european parliament decided, and, in any policy which is dependent on the market, price volatility is an inevitable feature. the last two years have tested the adequacy or otherwise of the measures, and we need – as several speakers have said here this evening – to work together to ensure that farmers are provided with the appropriate tools to deal with price volatility, and we need to learn and look at the market experience of the past two years in relation to what tools we require. in my opening remarks, i said that we must work at removing obstacles to the use of these market tools in the present cap. if, as mr dorfmann or mr de castro suggest, it is because of red tape, then we must make the policy simpler. simplification is something that i very much support, and i will do everything possible to reduce red tape in the agricultural sector, as i am already doing. of course it may also be – as ms girling said – that we have used all the tools that are available. if that is the case, we need collectively to be more imaginative and see if there are other proposals that we can make in this regard. next year’s communication provides an opportunity for this house and for the council, and i am committed to working constructively with all stakeholders to help our farmers in this regard. a number of speakers have referred to the need to ensure sustainable production, and i want to agree with mr ropė when he identifies small farmers as being central to the future of sustainable agricultural production and sustainable rural communities in europe. we need to ensure that farmers, who are our boots on the ground in the context of implementing environment and climate action, continue to be the custodians of our policy in our rural areas, and also the custodians of our rural environment. mr de castro also referred to the need to remove obstacles to such tools as the income stabilisation mechanism, and you and all members of the house will get an opportunity to assist me in a proposal in this regard in the omnibus regulation which is coming before the house in 2017. so i urge you to adopt this regulation, as mr dantin noted, to help farmers to get easier access to the income stabilisation tool and to get easier access to credit through the reforms that i am making and the changes in the financial instruments. despite any differences which may exist in this house and between our respective institutions, there is clear agreement across the board on the need to strengthen the position of farmers in the food chain and to tackle the issue of unfair trading practices. i agree with what mr tarabella said in this regard. i would also remind the house that the council adopted council conclusions yesterday, which, along with the overwhelming vote of this parliament, are making a very important statement and contribution towards the need for the commission to come forward with proposals in the work programme of 2017 to try to deal with this issue of the position of the farmer in the food chain. i should also say that, despite the support that farmers get from the european union and our national governments to co-finance programmes, most farmers would like to get their income from the market. that means having access to the market, and getting a fair return from the market. so we need fair trade, not always free trade, and farmers are benefitting from well negotiated free trade agreements and access to third—country markets. we are making good progress in this regard, and i am confident that this trend will continue. we cannot continue to have farmers’ production in storage at the expense of the european union taxpayer all the time. we have to find outlets for that, internally and externally. in terms of achieving a fair return, i welcome the report of the agricultural markets task force. the commission is currently considering those recommendations very carefully, and this will inform the proposal i will make in 2017. i would like to remind mr serrão santos, that farmers in the azores under the posei scheme are getting at up to eur 250 extra per cow in the dairy sector if they wish to utilise that, in addition to voluntary coupled support from the portuguese government. these are instruments that are already available and which are being utilised by your regional government and your national government in portugal in order to assist your dairy farmers. finally, i would like once again to express my appreciation to ms delahaye and the shadow rapporteurs for the work done in producing this report. this will serve as very important information and recommendations to me in the context of the work programme for 2017 and the legislative proposals and measures that we will bring forward in the context of the position of the farmer in the food chain.
in writing. the economic situation of european farms is unfortunately far from stabilising. this is largely due to the specific nature of the sector, which is more dependent on natural factors than any other and these are difficult to predict. in addition, there are issues of changes in international trade and local demand. all this leads to high price volatility, which has negative consequences for both food producers and consumers. we therefore need effective measures to reduce price fluctuations as much as possible. i share the rapporteur's view that the risk management support currently offered by the cap under the second pillar is insufficient. risk management instruments need to be reviewed and, where appropriate, developed. the objective of market transparency should also be pursued to the greatest extent possible. the overriding objective of these actions should be to guarantee a decent level of income for farmers and to create a stable market for goods for consumers.

the summit concludes a year of 2016 that was dominated by bad news from within and around the european union. the consolation prize may be news from the job market, which is indeed more alive than ever. the union has created eight million new jobs since 2013. another consolation may be the unexpected result of the british referendum in the form of increased trust in the european institutions. the agenda for the next summit is migration, security, opportunities for young people. it is indeed the decisive battlefield against populism and nationalism, which have been the cause of the greatest misery on our continent. in 2016, it has not only dictated the work programme, but also the tone of public debate, fears and the mood of europeans. i know it's not easy to dress up rational programs with emotions and get our message across to a younger generation who haven't felt firsthand the effects of nationalism and selfishness that have destroyed our continent. they are not a recipe for new, exciting visions, a re-imagining of europe. we have the right programmes, the slogans sound good too - valletta action plan, internal security strategy, defence union - but we have to prove that it works. the union must convince the average citizen of its usefulness, and that is what i wish for 2017.

in writing. ‒ i voted in favour of the motion on insolvency proceedings and trustees, as it directly concerns poland and the protection of its economic interests. in december 2015, poland notified the commission of a major reform of its national legislation on restructuring with effect from 1 january 2016 and requested amendments to the lists in the annexes to the regulation. the commission proposal and the proposed amendments are purely technical. they do not contain any substantive amendments to the regulation. therefore, the proposed proposal constitutes only a formal codification of the legislative text. it is important for poland to take urgent action on this issue, as it is clear that the failure to incorporate new types of proceedings quickly can have far-reaching negative financial consequences for cross-border creditors and debtors in polish restructuring and insolvency proceedings.
in writing. ‒ in december 2015, poland notified the commission of a major reform of its national legislation on restructuring with effect from 1 january 2016 and requested changes to the lists in annexes a and b to the regulation. the commission has examined whether the request submitted by poland complies with the requirements of the regulation and has presented a proposal to the european parliament and the council accordingly. the annexes to a regulation can only be amended by a regulation, which must be adopted in accordance with the ordinary legislative procedure, in accordance with the legal basis applied to the original regulation (article 81 tfeu). the proposal aims to ensure that the scope of the recast regulation is aligned with the actual legal framework. it is important for poland to act urgently on this issue, as it is clear that the failure to include new types of proceedings in the annexes to insolvency regulation no 1346/2000 quickly could have far-reaching negative financial consequences for cross-border creditors and debtors in polish restructuring and insolvency proceedings. i hereby endorse the report.

in writing. ‒ the accession of ecuador to the trade agreement between the european union and its member states, of the one part, and colombia and peru, of the other part, is an important step in the development of relations between the eu and ecuador, which has become an important regional partner with similar views. the agreement provides for the gradual opening of the market for goods, services, public procurement and investment, including the abolition of most tariffs. it therefore allows ecuador to maintain preferential access to the eu market, although the country is no longer eligible for gsp+ due to the fact that the world bank has reclassified it as an upper-middle income country. in addition, the agreement includes a chapter on trade and sustainable development, which includes ambitious provisions on labour and environmental protection and aims to guarantee predictable and stable environmental conditions for investors and operators on both sides. the agreement will allow both parties to develop even closer bilateral relations and will provide impetus for further economic and political integration in the andean region. it will also provide an opportunity to strengthen the political dialogue between the eu and ecuador based on respect for democratic principles and fundamental rights.

in writing. ‒ the agreement on mutual access to fishing grounds in the skagerrak and kattegat between denmark, norway and sweden has been in force since august 1967. the agreement allows these three countries to access each other's fish stocks beyond 4 nautical miles from their national baselines. denmark joined the eu in 1973 and sweden in 1995, so the commission became responsible for managing the agreement on behalf of these two member states. the agreement is currently being updated to reflect developments in international fisheries law. the agreement provides for: the maintenance of the exclusive access granted to vessels from denmark, norway and sweden to each other's waters outside the area of 4 nautical miles from baselines; support for conservation and management measures for fish stocks in this area; the possibility of applying control measures in accordance with the rules of the normal jurisdiction of the coastal state (this is already the case for fisheries in the north sea). i hereby endorse the report.

in writing. ‒ on 8 november 2016, the commission adopted a proposal for a decision to mobilise the egf in favour of spain in order to support the reintegration into the labour market of workers made redundant as a result of the bankruptcy and liquidation of bosal s.a., which has made the majority of the redundancies covered by this proposal and which is active in nace rev. 2 division 29 ( production of motor vehicles, trailers and semi-trailers) mainly in the region of valencia (comunidad valenciana es52), classified at nuts 2 level. the european globalisation adjustment fund (egf) was established to provide additional support to workers affected by the consequences of major structural changes in world trade patterns. in accordance with the provisions of article 12 of regulation (eu, euratom) no 1311/2013 establishing the multiannual financial framework for the years 2014-2020 and article 15 of regulation (eu) no 1309/2013, the fund's resources may not exceed a maximum annual amount of eur 150 million (in 2011 prices). the corresponding amounts shall be entered in the general budget of the union as a reserve. in accordance with point 13 of the interinstitutional agreement of 2 december 2013 between the european parliament, the council and the commission on budgetary discipline, on cooperation in budgetary matters and on sound financial management for the purpose of implementing the fund, where the application is approved, the commission shall submit to the budgetary authority a proposal to implement the fund and, at the same time, a corresponding proposal for the transfer of appropriations. i hereby endorse the report.

in writing. ‒ in view of the outdated nature and the unreasonableness of the application of the provisions of the regulation, i voted against the enf's proposal to reject the council's position. i am in favour of adopting the proposal to repeal council regulation (eec) no 1192/69 on common rules for the standardization of the accounts of railway undertakings. solutions for the compensation of costs incurred by railway undertakings were necessary in the 1960s when national railway undertakings acted on behalf of the state or another public authority. however, with the opening of the railway market and the separation of rail transport operations from infrastructure management, regulation (eec) no 1192/69 became incompatible with union law. the excessive number of regulations that are being deprecated should be reduced. compensation issues where they are still necessary and in accordance with union law should be incorporated into more relevant union legislation.
in writing. ‒ as regards the regulation on the standardisation of accounts, i support the repeal of this legal act, which aims to introduce greater transparency in the law applicable to the railway sector. compensatory payments made by the state to the infrastructure manager on the basis of the repealed regulation will be allowed on the basis of a different legal basis (article 8 of directive 2012/34/eu on the establishment of a single european railway area). i hereby endorse the compromise reached.
in writing. ‒ long-term provisions should be introduced, not as in the proposed interim document. the proposed rules are not very detailed and raise a number of legal doubts, especially as the current arrangements should be modern. that's why i didn't support the project.
in writing. ‒ i voted against the proposal to reject the council's position because i support the adoption of an agreement on the opening of national rail passenger markets and on the award of public service contracts, the so-called fourth railway package. i believe that the rail industry is a very important sector of the european union's economy, which brings benefits across borders and should therefore be encouraged. the agreement provides for the gradual opening of national rail passenger markets. this is the last segment of the rail transport market which has not yet been liberalised in most member states and is based mainly on direct award of public service contracts. it should be stressed that the public authorities will continue to be able to directly award public service contracts for rail services, provided that the service providers meet objective objectives and efficiency and effectiveness criteria.
in writing. ‒ i voted in favour of the report by mr van de campa because i support the general direction of the changes aimed at introducing a single railway market in europe. anyone who has had the opportunity to use trains in different european countries will be aware that there are still huge differences in both the quality and availability of services. this situation persists despite the efforts of the commission and the member states and despite some progress already made. however, it should be noted that this is due to a variety of reasons and that the quality and availability of rail passenger services is affected not only by the number of operators but also by the type of management, state support, the level of implementation of reforms and many other factors. i therefore believe that we must continue to work towards an appropriate level of competition, but this process must be balanced and the highest possible level of service must be maintained. the changes must be made with the passengers in mind, while at the same time improving the quality of the rolling stock, the service and the network, and reducing fares, which are still too high in many cases and make road transport more competitive.
in writing. ‒ i support the compromise solutions that have been worked out on the political pillar of the fourth railway package. as regards the pso regulation, i am pleased to maintain the possibility of direct award of contracts in exceptional cases, to maintain the favourable definition of 'local authorities', which will allow the local governments of the voivodships to directly award pso contracts to internal entities (to transport companies established by them, such as mazowieckie railways or wielkopolskie railways) the option of providing access to the rolling stock, ensuring the possibility of implementing long-term pso contracts already concluded (for the time they have been concluded). i hereby endorse the compromise reached.
in writing. ‒ the project has a number of errors which, when accumulated, give a negative picture of the changes. the basic mistake is that the railway is always a strategic state company. it is therefore up to each country to decide whether it wants to open up its industry to private capital. that's why i didn't support the proposed changes.
in writing. ‒ recognising the potential and untapped opportunities in the rail sector, i voted against the proposal to reject the council's position. i agree with the proposal to amend directive 2012/34/eu of the european parliament and of the council of 21 november 2012 on the establishment of a single european railway area with regard to the opening of the market for national rail passenger services and railway infrastructure management. i believe that the proposed changes will contribute to the development of the railway sector and will improve the quality of the services provided. the amendments to the directive cover a number of actions to increase the attractiveness, innovation and competitiveness of union rail transport. it provides for the establishment of a law giving european companies the possibility to operate throughout the eu and for stricter competition rules. the regulation introduces provisions to standardise the rules in the railway sector and to increase the transparency of the actions undertaken.
in writing. ‒ innovation in rail transport in the european union is a very important topic and needs to be approached with caution. the fourth railway package is about reform and in my view, it is a huge opportunity for the national railways of the member states. it is also a response to consumer needs, aimed at reducing travel costs, ensuring safety or opening up new routes. opening up rail transport to other countries could also lead to the creation of new railway companies that will help europe in an era of rising unemployment. the introduction of open tendering will give each carrier a chance to present its offer, which in my view is fair competition. the adoption of this package will also help to complete the process of creating a single railway area, which is why i voted in favour.
in writing. ‒ as regards the governance directive, i am pleased that there are no provisions requiring radical, costly and time-consuming structural changes to the railway market in poland, requiring full separation between the infrastructure manager and the railway undertakings and between the infrastructure manager and the maintenance companies, by favourably wording the definition of 'vertically integrated undertaking', excluding regional networks with a track gauge different from the dominant network of the member states in the eu (in the case of pkp lhs) from the scope of the directive, i.e. from the obligation to manage the infrastructure for the provision of rail services. i hereby endorse the compromise reached.
in writing. ‒ the fourth railway package, which was presented by the european commission, has a number of irregularities. the project introduces unnecessary bureaucracy and decision-making chaos. importantly, it does not contain detailed provisions that could reduce the entrepreneurial spirit of railway companies, which is why i voted against the project.
in writing. ‒ i voted in favour of the recommendation for second reading prepared by david-maria sassolego. i believe that these recommendations form a pragmatic pillar for the railway package. after several years of discussion, it was rightly agreed that, in addition to the common eu rules, the specificities of each country must be taken into account. in the case of poland, this means, for example, that regional undertakings which provide local transport services within individual voivodships are allowed to develop. this is very important for the many passengers who use local services to get to work, school or the doctor every day. however, this way of thinking should also lead to increased eu funding for local transport. the eu's investments, mainly in high-speed rail, will not solve other important social needs. these local, daily connections are what most people care about.
in writing. ‒ i voted in favour of the adoption of a regulation on the establishment of a legal framework for access to the market for port services and financial transparency for ports. i believe that the final proposal for amendments, as a result of a fair consensus, leads to greater access for service providers to the port services market and to the establishment of common rules on financial transparency and charges. it is particularly important for me that the regulations should provide for the widest possible powers for the member states. the amendments proposed by the ecr guarantee, inter alia, the removal of provisions empowering the commission to adopt delegated acts, the freedom to determine the most appropriate form of charging by ports, the possibility for member states to address the commission on the exclusion of private ports from the application of certain regulatory measures and the adequate protection of smaller ports from the negative effects of stringent rules.
in writing. ‒ after 15 years of work, a balanced report on market access to port services and financial transparency of ports has been adopted. i am glad that in the course of the work, and especially in this term of the european parliament, your rapporteur has been able to be persuaded to open up and accept the arguments of all the parties to the dialogue. one of the most important proposals is to recognise the autonomy and self-reliance of port authorities, while at the same time emphasising financial transparency, especially in the area of public aid. the important thing is that the 'one size fits all' approach has been abandoned, which is why i supported the report, as did most members.
in writing. ‒ in the course of the work on the regulation, solutions have been developed which are in the interests of poland, such as the elimination of the obligation to appoint an independent body to monitor and supervise the application of the regulation; the exclusion of transhipment terminals and passenger handling and piloting services from the main chapter of the proposed regulation - on the rules for the provision of port services and from the transitional provisions imposing the obligation to adapt the contracts governing port services to the new rules; the significant reduction of the scope of application of the regulation with regard to dredging services; the extension of the period of application of the regulation - up to 24 months from its publication; the exclusion of the power to issue implementing and delegated acts by the ec; in particular, the fact that the maritime regulation should not in any way infringe the legal systems governing port services in the member states and should allow for different structures to be applied in the member states. i hereby endorse the compromise reached.

in writing. ‒ i voted in favour of the draft amendment to the legal basis following the periodic evaluation of the rules for the management of the research fund for coal and steel. the fbip programme is a continuation of the treaty establishing the european coal and steel community (ecsc), which expired in 2002. the programme is financed by the proceeds from the sale of the remaining assets of the now defunct egtc. the fund provides around eur 50 million per year to finance research and development and innovation in the coal and steel sectors (72.8% for the steel sector and 27.2% for the coal sector). the research funded covers production processes, resource recovery and conservation, environmental improvement and occupational safety in the relevant sectors. the importance of financing is very important in relation to the nature of the polish raw material economy and the mining sector. this is linked to the possibility of developing knowledge and fostering innovation in a sector that is of great importance for poland.
