in writing. ‒ i abstained on the eu annual report on human rights and democracy in the world and the european union's human rights and democracy policy for 2015. i believe that the report, although it deals with very important issues relating to the protection of human rights, contains problematic sections in its substance which raise a number of questions. i am deeply convinced that development and human rights are interdependent and that respect for and protection of human rights are essential to reducing inequalities and achieving the sustainable development goals for all people. unfortunately, the discrepancies and the points of dispute in the report have led me to abstain from voting on the report.
in writing. ‒ i voted in favour of the adoption of the annual report on human rights and democracy in the world and the european union's human rights and democracy policy for 2015. we celebrated international human rights day a few days ago, so today's discussion on the state of human rights in 2015 is a perfect time to reflect on this topic. the universal declaration of human rights has been in force for nearly 70 years, but i feel that in the face of brutal conflicts and rising violence in the world, the collective struggle to uphold these rights has long since been less important and more necessary. issues such as the right to life and security, freedom of religion, assembly, and the prohibition of torture guarantee people a peaceful and dignified existence in their countries of residence and reduce the need for often dangerous and precarious migration. i therefore believe that the european union must fight with full energy and determination for the respect of universal human rights in the world. in this context, the effective implementation of the action plan for human rights and democracy 2015-2019 is of particular importance.
in writing. ‒ the comprehensive report on human rights and democracy in the world (2016/2219 (ini)) deserves to be appreciated and supported. the report highlights the importance of international agreements and institutions for ensuring respect for human rights, annual reports and reports prepared at the level of the european union, and the inclusion of human rights and democratic principles in the foreign policy negotiations of the eu member states and the union itself. the report draws attention to the victims of armed conflicts and refugees, and the importance of cooperation with countries of origin and transit, which allows migration policy to be implemented more efficiently, migration flows to be managed and the most vulnerable to be better protected. it called on the eu to encourage third countries to sign the palermo protocol against the smuggling of illegal immigrants and recalled the valletta summit agreements. the report addresses the situation of children, whose numbers are increasing among refugees, including unaccompanied children, and children who are missing or separated from their parents, and calls for adequate health, social and educational care and protection from violence. i support most of the comments and recommendations in the report and the call for member states to implement the eu action plan on human rights 2015-2019.
in writing. ‒ the report makes positive reference to assistance to internally displaced persons in ukraine and the protection of human rights defenders and journalists worldwide. but there are also many aspects that are problematic. unfortunately, much of the report also focuses on asylum and migration, and it instructs member states on family reunification and opening up legal migration routes. the report calls for, among other things, free and high-quality education, healthcare and housing for refugees, as well as access to the labour market. the section on women's rights calls for the right to access safe and legal abortion. in view of the comparable number of positive and negative aspects of the report, i abstained.
in writing. ‒ protecting human rights and promoting democracy in the world are priorities not only for the european parliament but also for the european union as a whole. the beliefs in this area are many and without increased efforts on the part of the member states and the community, it will not be possible to effectively place human rights and democratic values at the centre of their relations with their foreign partners. to ensure that human rights continue to be mainstreamed in the external aspects of eu policies, particular emphasis must be placed on those areas that require renewed political commitment and additional efforts to support local actors. it is also essential to prevent and redress human rights violations during conflicts and armed crises. the european union needs to be more coherent in its response to such strategic policy areas as migration, trade and the fight against terrorism, and to deepen the effectiveness and improve the performance of the union's human rights instruments. the challenges to human rights in key areas such as freedom of expression, non-discrimination, gender equality and the promotion of economic, social and cultural rights are enormous. while supporting the report, i also expect the european union to make a more determined effort.
in writing. ‒ the report makes positive reference to assistance to internally displaced persons in ukraine and the protection of human rights defenders and journalists worldwide. unfortunately, the report's themes overlap to a very large extent with those of the libe committee, which is largely concerned with asylum and migration. the report also advises eu member states on family reunification and opening up legal migration routes. i abstained from the vote.
in writing. ‒ the issue of human rights is one of the eu's priorities, which is why an annual review of eu policy in this area is important and much needed. as chair of the ep delegation for relations with belarus, i pay particular attention to the human rights situation in belarus. unfortunately, it's not a good one. belarus is the last country in europe to use the death penalty. in november, more executions were carried out. i am glad that the situation in belarus has not escaped the attention of this report. the european parliament will consistently call on the belarusian authorities to adopt a moratorium on the use of the death penalty, which is the first step in the process of its total abolition. the activities of the eu special representative for human rights, stavros lambrinidis, are also very important in this context. i look forward to a fruitful cooperation in this area.
in writing. ‒ in order to protect the sovereignty of the member states and the inviolability of their competence in the field of foreign and security policy, i abstained from the vote on the implementation of the common foreign and security policy. the lisbon treaty sought to increase the coherence and visibility of the common foreign and security policy. the development of the common security and defence policy, the creation of the european external action service and the establishment of the high representative of the union for foreign affairs and security policy are a continuation of this strategy to strengthen the eu's role on the world stage. given the current volatile situation of the terrorist threat and the real risk of war in europe, i believe that the eu's foreign and security policy can be an important tool for the pursuit of multilateral, shared interests. however, i also believe that it cannot replace the possibility for member states who decide to do so to pursue their own independent policy in these areas.
in writing. ‒ the report presents the cfsp in the context of the current crisis situations in the eu's neighbourhood and beyond, and assesses current and future threats to european security and aspirations. the rapporteur welcomes the eu as a global power and a forerunner of international diplomacy, and calls on the member states to stop looking at foreign and security policy from a 'limited national perspective'. the rapporteur calls for a strengthening of the cfsp based on the three pillars defence, deterrence and response while calling for a similar strengthening of the common security and defence policy (csdp). the report made a number of other recommendations, including the development of a defence white paper, increased parliamentary scrutiny of the cfsp, strengthening the eu/eea diplomatic arm, and a review of eu relations with russia. i believe that the eu's foreign and security policy can be an important tool for pursuing multilateral, shared interests. however, we also believe that it can never replace the ability of a member state to pursue its own independent policy in these areas, as soon as it decides to do so. i hereby abstain from voting.
in writing. ‒ the european union today faces unprecedented internal and external challenges, including interstate conflicts, state collapse, terrorism, hybrid threats, cyber and energy insecurity, and organised crime. unfortunately, these conflicts have direct and serious consequences for the security and well-being of european citizens, as they increasingly engulf the eu, whether in the form of terrorism, mass movements of refugees or disinformation campaigns designed to divide our societies. however, this situation also provides an opportunity to improve the way the eu works and to strengthen cooperation between member states. without strong national commitment, co-responsibility, political will and leadership, the eu's common foreign, security and defence policy cannot be effectively implemented. of course, there is no doubt that nato is the foundation of collective security in europe. however, the declaration on cooperation between nato and the eu adopted at the warsaw summit is welcome. i fully support deeper cooperation between nato and the eu on security, as a stronger nato and a stronger eu reinforce and complement each other.
in writing. ‒ the report presents the cfsp in the context of the current crisis situations in the eu's neighbourhood and beyond, and assesses current and future threats to european security and aspirations. e. brok welcomes the eu as a global power and a forerunner of international diplomacy, and calls on the member states to stop looking at foreign and security policy from a 'limited national perspective'. i believe that the eu's foreign and security policy can be an important tool for pursuing multilateral, shared interests. but it cannot replace the ability of a member state to conduct its own foreign and security policy. i abstained from the vote.
in writing. ‒ the elmar brok report is an important document because it provides a holistic view of the community's foreign policy. the analysis of the situation is reliable, in-depth, but also critical in many places. it is important that the union institutions are able to assess their own actions objectively, including those that have not been entirely successful. i am pleased to draw attention to the problem of disinformation by third countries and to the need to counter this phenomenon. this also includes the threat of cyberattacks. here too, we need to do more to protect data and ensure that we have a secure and sustainable access to the network. i welcome the strong declaration of support for the eu enlargement process and for close cooperation with the eastern partnership and the balkan countries. strong defence is listed as one of the three pillars of the eu's external action. the so-called defence package presented in november is a step in the right direction. i hope that we will not end up once again creating and accepting a good description of reality, which is not something that community policy makers can do much about.
in writing. ‒ i abstained from the vote on the report on the instruments of the common agricultural policy to limit price volatility on agricultural markets, as the amendment to the report submitted by the polish delegation to the ecr was not taken into account. amendment which emphasises that direct payments should remain an instrument of the cap after 2020. the rejection of the amendment, while recognising the potential of long-term contracts and the possibility of blocking production prices for a certain period of time in order to neutralise the impact of volatility, was decisive for my decision in this case.
in writing. ‒ the concept of price volatility in agriculture means significant changes in the prices of agricultural products in a given year. farmers often face significant price fluctuations for their agricultural products. this creates financial uncertainty for farmers' incomes and may put them at risk, as their incomes are less predictable and they may be exposed to sudden price falls. in addition, this phenomenon reduces the opportunities for long-term investment, especially by young farmers. agriculture is also exposed to price volatility due to climatic and weather factors and changes in world trade, especially with russia and china, and the resulting surplus of goods on the european market. the amendment submitted by the pis delegation, which emphasised that direct payments should remain an instrument of the cap after 2020, was considered by the rapporteur to be inconsistent with the report and was rejected. i hereby abstain from voting.
in writing. ‒ agricultural activity is dependent on biological processes and therefore highly dependent on climatic conditions and plant and animal diseases. of course, these natural factors are beyond the farmer's control. however, price volatility is increasingly affected by factors such as the instability and imperfection of agricultural markets, greater supply volatility due to climate instability, and fragile food supply imbalances. the change in profitability for agricultural holdings is therefore more difficult to predict than for enterprises in other sectors of the economy. a more explicit and coherent policy strategy, with targeted instruments at union and national level, is therefore necessary to ensure a multifunctional, sustainable agricultural production across the union. in particular, further development of climate, health and economic risk management instruments, in particular the different types of agricultural production insurance or individual reserve and mutual investment fund mechanisms, is necessary to limit the effects of price volatility and to support future farm management. it is equally important to take action to raise the awareness of farmers and agricultural organisations of the opportunities for modernisation and to increase the competitiveness of farms.
in writing. ‒ direct payments should remain an instrument of the common agricultural policy beyond 2020. unfortunately, the rapporteur considered this case to be inconsistent with the report. i therefore abstained.
madam president, commissioner, the greek economy has been in crisis for eight years, being unable to return to sustainable growth. a lot of blame for this unprecedented failure is routinely put on the european institutions and the so-called austerity measures, but the truth is that the necessary structural reforms in greece have never been fully implemented. they have been incomplete, partial and delayed, and the damage has been further exacerbated by unrealistic promises made by populist politicians. if economic growth is to be restored, more flexibility is needed in the labour market. the eu should stand ready to help greece with the european youth initiatives and programmes aimed at increasing mobility and employability, but the responsibility for implementing reforms is entirely on the greek government. let me repeat once again that there is no obligation for greece to accept financial assistance from outside. but if greece wants to use other countries’, other member states’ taxpayers’ money, it has to reform in order to guarantee that this money is repaid back on time. (the speaker agreed to take a blue-card question under rule 162(8))
blue-card answer. – yes, thank you for your question. of course i am of the opinion that greece should be subject to the same rules as other countries. that includes also the rules of the stability and growth pact, which are the rules, by the way, that greece has violated for a number of years. now, on the other hand, as far as the reforms are concerned, as i said, they have been implemented late and slowly, and this is the reason for the lack of result. if you want to have, indeed, conditions conducive for investment, as you are interested in, and more job creation, we have to be consistent in implementing those reforms.
in writing. ladies and gentlemen! the situation of the greek labour market is the worst in the union. despite some progress, more than 23% of the country's citizens are still unemployed, and nearly 17% have been out of work for more than a year. most worryingly, however, nearly half of young greeks are not in permanent employment. so it's good that last week we were able to reach an agreement on the extension of the loan repayment period by athens and the waiver of some of the interest. it has long been known that without debt restructuring, greece will not be able to return to growth. however, the entry into force of the agreement is conditional on athens implementing labour market reforms, which may contribute to further unemployment growth in the short term. i understand the concerns of the people of this country, who after years of sacrifice still see no clear prospect of improvement. but i come from a country that, in the midst of an economic transformation, had to make radical changes to its labour market, which resulted in massive unemployment. greece, like poland in the early 1990s, has no other way and certain decisions must be taken. it is necessary to support the government in athens with the decision to restructure the debt. without it, as the international monetary fund has already pointed out, the situation in that country will not improve.

member of the commission. – madam president, on behalf of the commission i would like to thank the rapporteur, ms vallina, for her interesting and comprehensive report on the work of the committee on petitions in 2015. like its predecessors, the report bears witness to the breadth of issues that petitioners bring to the attention of the committee on petitions each year and to the committee’s efforts to ensure that the voices of those petitioners are heard. the commission agrees that the right to petition has to be a key element for our participatory democracy, in which the right of every citizen to play a direct part in the democratic life of the union is effectively protected. as my colleague, frans timmermans, stated in his last exchange of views with the committee in april, petitions are one of the few instruments where the institutions come into direct contact with citizens. at a time when europe is facing many challenges, such direct contacts with citizens are more important than ever. the citizens who turn to the committee for help feel in many cases that they have exhausted all other avenues. they are real people with real problems. if we are to have any chance of bridging the gap that seems to have opened up between european institutions and the public, it is crucial that we – and by ‘we’ i mean the commission and parliament – can demonstrate that we take citizens’ seriously and show them what solutions exist at european or at national level. as the statistics in the report make clear, the commission remains the committee on petitions’ principal partner when it comes to handling petitions. of the petitions that are not closed in the early stages of the procedure, nearly 90% are referred to the commission for an opinion. i am therefore pleased to have this opportunity to reaffirm the commission’s commitment to providing the committee on petitions with meaningful replies to each request for an opinion, and to do so in a timely manner. the commission also remains committed to sending its most competent officials to the committee’s meetings to ensure that the committee and the petitioners receive the latest information and proper explanations of the issues under discussion. this is perhaps the right moment to turn to one of the issues raised by you, ms vallina, in your report, namely the commission’s interpretation of article 51 of the charter of fundamental rights. i know that this issue has been raised in previous reports and is one where many members of this house consider that the commission’s interpretation is unduly narrow. it is clear that the charter’s scope has its limitations. defined by the treaty, they result from the principle of conferral of powers, a cornerstone of the european union. however, as reflected in the report, the charter is one element of the architecture of fundamental rights protection in europe. it complements national systems for fundamental rights protection, but does not replace them. the commission shares your concerns about how to ensure that citizens’ expectations as regards the protection of their fundamental rights are upheld. the commission attaches particular importance to increasing individuals’ understanding of how they can avail themselves of their fundamental rights, and whom to approach to enforce them. it is crucial to dispel misunderstandings and avoid raising false expectations. a concrete step in this direction was the introduction last october, in the e-justice portal, of a fundamental rights page, which helps individuals seeking to enforce their fundamental rights to identify the competent national non—judicial bodies with a human rights remit. the commission will also make the best possible use of existing financial programmes to empower civil society organisations and human rights bodies, which work on raising awareness about the charter and ensuring its application at national level. let me thank ms vallina once again for her report. i look forward to hearing the views of honourable members.
on behalf of the s&d group. the subject of the 2015 annual report is the review of the work of the committee on petitions, which allows any citizen of the european union, acting individually or in association with others, to exercise at any time his or her right to lodge a complaint with the european parliament under article 227 of the treaty on the functioning of the european union. the 2015 annual statistics show that the majority of petitioners turn to parliament for help on matters relating to the environment, justice, the internal market and fundamental rights. last year, parliament received over 1400 petitions, a drop of as much as 47% compared to 2014. unfortunately, the report does not examine the reasons for this state of affairs. of the petitions received, 943 were considered admissible and 483 were considered inadmissible. the percentage of inadmissible petitions has decreased by more than 6% compared to 2014, while the percentage of petitions considered admissible has increased by almost 6%, which shows that citizens have a better understanding of our competences. the committee on petitions also managed to eliminate the existing delays in the examination of petitions in 2015. the european commission remains the largest partner of the committee on petitions in dealing with complaints that are not closed at an early stage of the procedure and that are almost 90% referred for consideration and opinion to the european commission. in 2015, the spanish petitioners were the most numerous, followed by italians, germans, romanians and poles. the rapporteur, ms ángela vallina, has produced a very good report, and i congratulate her and thank her for the effective cooperation.
the committee on petitions is the only committee in the european parliament that guarantees direct contact with citizens. it only takes one vote from a citizen or the president, in the form of an email or a letter, to petition, because the treaties on european union allow the european parliament to be consulted on various problems that citizens encounter in their daily lives, provided that the issues raised are within the scope of the european union's activities. every month we examine such petitions in the presence of the petitioners, and in this way, as members of parliament, we can learn about the difficulties in implementing eu law in the member states. we therefore work with the european commission, the council, the european ombudsman, the legal service and member state authorities at various levels. as a committee, we also organise public hearings and go on observation missions. in the context of the annual report on the activities of the committee on petitions, i would like to highlight a few aspects. first, our priority should be to deal with petitions within a reasonable timeframe to avoid leaving petitions unresolved for too long. secondly, we should streamline the process of examining petitions by digitalising the procedure, making it easier for both members and the committee secretariat. and the last point is very important, because we must ensure that the issues under discussion are really european law and not a tool for political struggle. very often, political parties during election campaigns have tried to use the commission as a tool in the struggle for political votes in recent years. we must say clearly and firmly no. we do not agree to this. in writing. ‒ i voted in favour of the proposal for a regulation of the european parliament and of the council amending regulation (ec) no 539/2001 listing the third countries whose nationals must be in possession of visas when crossing the external borders and those whose nationals are exempt from that requirement (amending the suspension mechanism). i believe that the compromise reached in the negotiations on the amendments serves to strengthen the strategy related to migration policy. the union's visa policy is a core policy area of the european union with implications for both external action and internal security. it is necessary to amend the suspension mechanism for visa procedures in order to make it more efficient and flexible. this will allow the eu to respond to specific circumstances resulting from a sudden and significant increase in the inflow of third-country nationals staying illegally in the eu, as well as unjustified asylum applications and rejected readmission applications. in order to guarantee respect for the rights of third-country nationals and the rules of the common visa policy, a robust set of guarantees should be established, as well as a system of reports and statistics provided by the european agency and by the relevant law enforcement authorities.
in writing. ‒ the main objective of this proposal is to strengthen the suspension mechanism by making it easier for member states to notify circumstances leading to a possible suspension and by enabling the commission to trigger the mechanism on its own initiative. the agreement reached reflects a solution between the council and parliament based on a three-step approach. 1) the european commission will adopt an implementing act on the temporary suspension of the exemption from the visa requirement for certain categories of third country nationals for a period of 9 months. if the circumstances persist during that period, the commission shall adopt a delegated act temporarily suspending the exemption from the visa requirement for all nationals of the third country concerned for a period of 18 months. before the expiry of the validity of the adopted delegated act, the european commission shall submit a report to the european parliament and to the council, which may be accompanied by a legislative proposal to amend this regulation in order to transfer the reference to the third country concerned from annex ii to annex i. i support the need for a suspension mechanism to be in place and strengthened in order to maintain confidence in future and existing agreements liberalising visa rules. such a standstill clause is also important because it allows for an efficient response to any emergency situation and does not require waiting for a solution in the legislative process.
in writing. ‒ the main objective of the proposal is to strengthen the suspension mechanism by making it easier for member states to notify circumstances leading to a possible suspension and by enabling the commission to trigger the mechanism on its own initiative. the need to maintain and strengthen the suspension mechanism in order to maintain confidence in future and existing agreements liberalising visa rules is worth supporting. such a standstill clause is also important because it allows for an efficient response to any emergency situation and does not require waiting for a solution in the legislative process. i therefore supported the report.
in writing. ‒ i voted against the draft implementing directive which aims to amend annexes iv to council directive 2000/29/ec. i believe that stricter controls on citrus imports will increase the risk of complaints to the wto and impose disproportionate and unjustified requirements on exporting countries where there have been no problems so far. in addition, the proposed changes, which aim to ensure more rigorous controls, go beyond the recommendations of efsa (european food safety authority). the sensible approach to protecting the market for citrus processing is to act by means of exceptional measures rather than a general tightening of measures. by the proposed amendments concerning the use of the thaumatotibia leucotreta freezing process only, the directive will lead to the suspension of research and prevent the use of new scientific processes.
in writing. ‒ tighter import controls on citrus fruits increase the risk of wto litigation and impose disproportionate and unjustified requirements on exporting countries that have not previously had any problems. the proposed changes also go beyond the recommendations of efsa. in the case of ongoing acquisitions involving third countries, this problem should be addressed through exceptional measures rather than through a general tightening of measures. as regards the restriction to the use of the freezing process alone, it is particularly mandatory and would prevent the study and application of new scientific processes. i voted against the resolution.
in writing. ‒ given the plight of women affected by the adverse effects of thalidomide, i voted in favour of a resolution guaranteeing support for victims of the drug. thalidomide was used to treat nausea in pregnant women, as well as headaches, insomnia and colds in the late 1950s and 1960s. it caused deformities in the foetus, particularly in the form of shortened limbs or the absence of limbs. the commission is also proposing to extend the scope of the directive to include the use of the term 'competent authority' in the definition of a public authority. the seriousness of the problem is underlined by the fact that this case was one of the main reasons for the adoption of eu rules on pharmaceutical industry supervision. i fully support the resolution calling for the coordination of actions to support victims in their compensation efforts, the strengthening of actions in individual countries (such as germany or spain) and the establishment of a european support programme, and calling on the company producing the medicine (grünenthal gmbh) to admit fault and pay the compensation due.
in writing. ‒ the resolution on the victims of thalidomide, a drug prescribed to pregnant women in the 1950s that caused foetal developmental disorders resulting in, among other things, no arms in children born later, sheds new light on the victims of this once poorly understood drug. they live not only in france but also in germany, sweden, the united kingdom, spain, italy and other eu countries. the resolution recalls the effects of thalidomide and the responsibilities of states in this regard. calls on the member states to provide adequate legal treatment and adequate social and medical care to thalidomide victims, many of whom live in poverty and without the necessary assistance; i believe that the history of thalidomide use should be taken into account when approving procedures for safety testing and marketing of medicinal products; the issues of risk and liability must be clearly defined. this history should also help to develop research and education on the physiology and pathology of pregnancy, to increase access to prenatal and perinatal healthcare, and to disseminate knowledge on pregnancy prevention so that such stories do not happen again in the future.
in writing. ‒ thalidomide was used to treat nausea in pregnant women, as well as headaches, insomnia and colds in the late 1950s and 1960s. the drug was used for several years before serious side effects were observed. it caused deformities in the foetus, particularly in the form of shortened limbs or the absence of limbs. this has happened in many member states and victims are still not adequately protected financially to cope with the rising costs of treatment. this case was one of the main reasons for the adoption of eu legislation on pharmaceutical industry supervision. the resolution calls for coordination of actions to support victims in their compensation efforts, for improvements in national actions (i.e. germany or spain), for the establishment of a european support programme and calls on the company producing the drug (grünenthal gmbh) to admit fault and pay appropriate compensation. for these reasons, i voted in favour of the resolution.

in writing. ‒ i voted in favour of the proposal for a revision of the paediatric regulation, which entered into force on 26 january 2007. i believe that this is necessary in view of the shortcomings identified in the implementation of the regulation, such as delays in clinical trials, paediatric oncology or the low number of new medicines authorised for marketing. the review of the regulation should give due weight to models of priority of medicinal products, earlier and easier clinical trials and more effective incentives to stimulate research, and serve the objectives of paediatric drug development.
in writing. ‒ i voted to reject the 2015 annual report on the results of the committee on petitions' deliberations, due to differences and lack of consensus on the content of the report. the committee's work programme is not linked to the european commission's legislative work programme, but is drawn up by citizens exercising their right to petition parliament and to share their concerns about specific areas of eu policy and legislation. i believe that the report should be amended in order to remove the inconsistencies in the opinion. the failure to incorporate the amendments submitted by ecr experts contributed to the negative assessment of the report.
in writing. ‒ i have supported the draft resolution on international aviation agreements, recognising the validity of the solutions proposed. the increasing importance of the air safety agreements with japan and china and the air communication agreements with china, turkey, mexico, the six member states of the gulf cooperation council, armenia and asean requires the development of negotiating guidelines before the start of negotiations. i believe that the role and commitment of the european parliament is such that it should be informed immediately and fully at all stages of the negotiations. from the very beginning of the procedure, parliament should receive regular and, where necessary, confidential full information on the procedure under way at all stages of the negotiations.
on behalf of the ecr group. mr president, i would like to thank you for your kind words. the union's customs policy is a major challenge for the commission and the european union as a whole. on the one hand, customs policy is intended to combat mainly illicit trade, organised crime, fraud and terrorism, while at the same time facilitating legal trade and providing citizens and businesses with a sense of security. the resolution calls for the eu's customs policy to be simplified, streamlined, made coherent and fair, while ensuring that customs duties are effective and uniformly enforced. the idea is that in the delegated acts to the customs code, the european commission should only propose proportionate rules that are intended to facilitate legitimate trade and the development of european competitiveness on a global scale, and not be additional administrative barriers. here are two examples of how these barriers are created. financial guarantee requirements for so-called authorised aeo's who already follow strict rules according to many companies these requirements should be abolished. furthermore, simplified customs procedures for low value consignments at import and export should be maintained. the european commission, on the other hand, proposes to withdraw the existing customs simplifications. this is contrary to the objectives of the digital single market to enable consumers and businesses to have better access to goods and services. the ecr group therefore supports the text of the resolution, which is intended to encourage the european commission to engage more closely with the business community and to work together to create a modern, coordinated, transparent, fair, consistent, predictable and secure eu customs code for citizens and businesses.
